findings.title: Main support-recovery resolution is information-theoretically impossible
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2014__accepted__v15-anandkumar14a__I01 — Main support-recovery resolution is information-theoretically impossible
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem 1 (Main Result), PDF page 3 / journal page 2241, equations (3)–(4); discussion PDF page 4; Assumptions A1–A6 and Theorems 5/7, PDF pages 29–31 / journal pages 2267–2269, equations (25)–(37); Procedure 3, PDF page 27; proof of Theorem 7, PDF page 50 / journal page 2288.

**Claim.** Under the homogeneous mixed-membership stochastic-block model with iid Dirichlet memberships, diagonal connectivity p and off-diagonal q<p, the stated sample-size and separation conditions suffice for simultaneous support recovery with high probability:

\[
 \Pi(i,j)\geq\xi\implies\widehat S(i,j)=1,\qquad
 \Pi(i,j)\leq\xi/2\implies\widehat S(i,j)=0
 \quad\text{for every }i,j.
\]

The support threshold is specified as \(\xi=\Omega(\varepsilon_P)\), where the claimed connectivity-estimation error is
\[
 \varepsilon_P=\widetilde O\left((\alpha_0+1)^{3/2}k\sqrt p/\sqrt n\right).
\]
There is no inverse power of p−q in this threshold. The paper defines high probability as probability \(1-n^{-c}\) for some c>0 (PDF 30).

**Error and evidence.** Consider the following sequence entirely within the homogeneous sparse-Dirichlet model:
\[
 k=2,\quad\alpha=(1/4,1/4),\quad\alpha_0=1/2,\quad
 p=1/2,\quad q=1/2-\delta_n,\quad\delta_n=n^{-1/4},\quad
 \xi_n=n^{-3/8}.
\]
Both individual Dirichlet parameters are below one, the normalized means are equal, P is full rank for every finite n, and its smallest eigenvalue is \(\delta_n>0\). Assumptions A2/A3 hold with polynomial slack: n exceeds every fixed polylogarithmic multiple of the constant sample-size requirement, and \(\delta_n\sqrt n=n^{1/4}\) exceeds every fixed polylogarithmic separation requirement. A5 permits \(\tau=\Theta(n^{-1/4})\). The advertised \(\varepsilon_P\) rate is \(\widetilde O(n^{-1/2})\), and \(\xi_n/n^{-1/2}=n^{1/8}\), so A6 is satisfied regardless of the fixed constants and polylogarithms in that rate. Grant the method unlimited iterations: the apparent double-log typo in A4 is not used in this counterexample.

An impossibility argument applies even if an estimator is given the true P and all but one membership vector. Write that node's membership as (t,1−t), and another node's as (s,1−s). Conditional on these memberships, each directed incident edge has probability
\[
 r(t,s)=q+\delta_n\{1-s+t(2s-1)\}.
\]
The model gives independent edges conditional on memberships; \(|\partial r/\partial t|\leq\delta_n\), and r lies in [1/4,1/2] for sufficiently large n. We must distinguish
\[
 I_0=[\xi_n/4,\xi_n/2]\quad\text{(required support bit 0)},\qquad
 I_1=[\xi_n,2\xi_n]\quad\text{(required support bit 1)}.
\]
For any \(t_0\in I_0,t_1\in I_1\), \(|t_0-t_1|\leq7\xi_n/4\). Using
\(D_{KL}(\operatorname{Ber}(u)\Vert\operatorname{Ber}(v))\leq(u-v)^2/[v(1-v)]\), summing over at most 2(n−1) directed incident edges gives
\[
 D_{KL}(\mathcal L(G\mid t_0,\Pi_{-J},P)\Vert
                 \mathcal L(G\mid t_1,\Pi_{-J},P))
 \leq(98/3)n\delta_n^2\xi_n^2\longrightarrow0.
\]
Nonincident edges have identical conditional laws and supply no further information about t. A conservative bound \(64n\delta_n^2\xi_n^2=64n^{-1/4}\) also accommodates a self-loop if included. Mixture convexity and Pinsker therefore bound the total variation distance between the conditional low-interval and high-interval observation laws by
\[
 v_n\leq\sqrt{32n^{-1/4}}\longrightarrow0.
\]

This is not an event too rare to contradict an all-node high-probability assertion. Here \(t\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1/4,1/4)\), and
\[
 \Pr(t\in I_0\cup I_1)=\Theta(\xi_n^{1/4}),\qquad
 n\xi_n^{1/4}=n^{29/32}\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
With probability tending to one, some node falls in the union. An oracle selects the first such node J, reveals J, P and every other true membership, and tells the estimator that tJ is in the union, without telling it the interval. Independence of the node memberships preserves the beta prior restricted to the union at J: knowing that earlier nodes are outside the union supplies no extra information about tJ. The low/high conditional prior weights converge respectively to
\[
 w_0=\frac{2^{-1/4}-4^{-1/4}}
 {2^{-1/4}-4^{-1/4}+2^{1/4}-1}=\sqrt2-1,
 \qquad w_1=2-\sqrt2.
\]
For any binary test, its Bayes error is at least \(\min(w_{0,n},w_{1,n})(1-v_n)\), tending to \(\sqrt2-1\approx0.4142\). This lower bound applies to an estimator given strictly more information than Procedure 3 receives.

Global label permutation does not evade the contradiction. With probability tending to one there are also oracle-known anchor nodes with t≤ξn/8 and t≥1−ξn/8, because their expected counts also grow as nξn^(1/4). Their required support patterns are respectively (0,1) and (1,0). On simultaneous support success the estimated communities can be aligned using these anchors. Correct all-node recovery would then produce a correct low/high test at J. Consequently any estimator's simultaneous support-success probability is at most \(2-\sqrt2+o(1)\approx0.5858\), rather than tending to one.

The unsupported proof step is visible directly on PDF 50. From absolute edge-profile error \(|\widehat F-F|=O(\varepsilon_P)\) and \(F_{j,i}=q+\Pi_{i,j}(p-q)\), a membership gap of size ξ produces an edge-profile gap of size (p−q)ξ. The argument drops this factor when concluding that ξ=Ω(εP) suffices. Keeping the factor would require at least a separation-dependent threshold such as \(\xi=\Omega(\varepsilon_P/(p-q))\), with the appropriate constants/logarithms. This observation locates the error; the information bound above independently disproves the published conclusion.

**Reason for rejection.** Zero-error recovery of significant overlapping memberships at the quantified threshold is expressly part of the main theorem and its explanation on PDF 4, not an incidental lemma. In the stated class, the claimed resolution cannot be achieved by any estimator, even with true parameters and an oracle revealing the other memberships. Restoring a separation factor changes the advertised membership resolution by the unbounded factor n^(1/4) on this family. It therefore withdraws a central recovery claim and materially changes the result being accepted. Separate tensor/parameter bounds and the pure stochastic-block special case are not disproved by this issue.

**Discovery method.** Tracing Procedure 3 and the support proof raised the question of how an absolute error in F could imply a membership threshold independent of p−q. Comparing the claimed resolution with the incident-edge information for one nearly pure node suggested the counterexample.

**Verification method.** Read the complete original PDF and appendices; rechecked the original rendered main theorem, assumptions, procedure and proof, including PDF pages 3/4/27/29/30/31/50. Derived the uniform Bernoulli KL bound, beta interval weights and oracle argument independently. The reproducible 350-digit script `support-certificate.py` in the audit evidence directory checks six network scales, 120 pairwise KL cases, interval-mass inequalities and the resulting Bayes bounds. An independent bounded second review re-read the original relevant pages and confirmed the assumptions, derivation and central-theorem scope; it did not replace the full-paper review.

**Confidence.** High mathematical confidence; high confidence that this meets the specified rejection standard. The argument is an asymptotic all-assumptions impossibility proof with polynomial slack over suppressed logarithms. Numerical checks supplement it rather than stand in for the proof. No claim is made that the historical external experiments failed or that every other result is false.

Audit evidence: an unpublished audit file contains the certificate, results, complete coverage notes, original extracted pages and independent bounded QA.

sections.title: Claim in the paper
sections.html: The main theorem recovers all sufficiently large overlapping memberships at the stated threshold.
sections.markdown: The main theorem recovers all sufficiently large overlapping memberships at the stated threshold.

sections.title: What may be wrong
sections.html: The threshold can demand distinctions that the observed edges do not contain enough information to make, even if an oracle reveals the other model parameters.
sections.markdown: The threshold can demand distinctions that the observed edges do not contain enough information to make, even if an oracle reveals the other model parameters.

sections.title: Evidence in brief
sections.html:
The audit uses two communities. As the node count n increases, their edge probabilities become closer, while the membership threshold remains within the theorem’s allowed regime:

\[ p=\frac12,\qquad q=\frac12-n^{-1/4},\qquad \xi=n^{-3/8}. \]

The information separating two required support labels tends to zero. Even with oracle assistance, the probability of recovering every required label is at most 2−√2 plus a vanishing term, rather than approaching one.

findings.title: The central correlated-regressor MSE oracle does not converge to the ARD limit
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2014__accepted__v15-aravkin14a__I01 — The central correlated-regressor MSE oracle does not converge to the ARD limit
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Proposition 15, equation (36), PDF page 20 / journal page 236; its weighted-MSE definition on PDF page 19 / journal page 235; Lemma 13, equations (28)–(30), PDF page 18 / journal page 234. The affected interpretation is repeated immediately after Proposition 15 and in Section 5.4, PDF page 22; introduction contribution (iii), PDF page 3, advertises the extension to correlated regressors.

**Claim.** For fixed true parameters \(\bar\theta\) and general random regressors satisfying the positive-definite covariance and empirical-Gram conditions, fix the other hyperparameters to bounded sequences with \(n\lambda_{nj}\to\infty\) for their nonzero true groups. Proposition 15 asserts that the hyperparameter minimizing the indicated \(d_{k,n}^4\)-weighted conditional-noise MSE for group i converges to
\[
 \|\bar\theta^{(i)}\|^2/k_i,
\]
the same limit claimed for ARD when \(\gamma=0\). This is a frequentist risk at a fixed truth, not an average over the fitted prior.

**Error and evidence.** Take two scalar groups, \(k_1=k_2=1\), noise variance \(\sigma^2=1\), true \(\bar\theta=(1,1)^\top\), and fix the other group's hyperparameter \(\lambda_{n2}=1\). Generate iid rows of G as \((E,ET)\), where E is an independent uniform sign and T is a sign with probabilities \(\Pr(T=1)=3/4\), \(\Pr(T=-1)=1/4\). These rows have zero mean and positive-definite covariance
\[
 \Psi=\begin{pmatrix}1&1/2\\1/2&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Their sample Gram is exactly
\[
 G^\top G=n\begin{pmatrix}1&c_n\\c_n&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad c_n\longrightarrow1/2\quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
Thus the paper's empirical-Gram bounds hold with probability tending to one, and the bounded other-hyperparameter sequence satisfies \(n\lambda_{n2}=n\to\infty\). A ball of radius 3 centered at zero includes all relevant finite hyperparameter values. If a null group is desired explicitly, append an independent Rademacher third regressor, true coefficient zero and hyperparameter zero: the first two estimated coefficients and the calculation below remain identical, while the full design still has positive-definite population covariance.

Condition on G and write \(c=c_n\), \(L=\lambda_1>0\). The estimator in equation (5) is equivalently
\[
 \widehat\theta=(G^\top G+\operatorname{diag}(1/L,1))^{-1}G^\top y.
\]
For abbreviations
\[
 u=n+1,\quad h=nc,\quad K=n^2(1-c^2)+n,\quad
 V=n^3(1-c^2)+2n^2(1-c^2)+n,
\]
its first-coordinate bias is \(-(u/L-h)/(u/L+K)\), and its first-coordinate conditional variance is \(V/(u/L+K)^2\). Therefore its exact MSE is
\[
 R_n(L)=\frac{V+(u/L-h)^2}{(u/L+K)^2}.                 \tag{A}
\]

The weight does not change this minimizer. In equation (28), \(\Sigma_{\bar v}^{(1)}=I+G_2G_2^\top\) explicitly excludes the varied hyperparameter L. The sole singular value obeys
\[
 d_{1,n}^2=\frac1nG_1^\top(I+G_2G_2^\top)^{-1}G_1
          =\frac{n(1-c^2)+1}{n+1}>0,
\]
so the weighted scalar-group risk is simply the positive L-independent factor \(d_{1,n}^4\) times (A).

Set \(z=u/L\). Differentiating \([V+(z-h)^2]/(z+K)^2\) gives a derivative whose sign is the sign of
\[
 (z-h)(K+h)-V.
\]
For c>0, it has exactly one positive zero, yielding the unique global minimizer
\[
 L_n^*=\frac{u(K+h)}{h(K+h)+V}
       \longrightarrow\frac1{1+c_n}\longrightarrow\frac23.
\]
This contradicts Proposition 15's asserted limit \(\bar\theta_1^2/k_1=1\). At c=1/2 the finite-n optimizer simplifies to
\[
 L_n^*=\frac{6n^2+18n+12}{9n^2+18n+8}.
\]
For example n=100 gives approximately 0.67327466, and n=1,000,000 gives 0.66666733. Symbolic calculation also gives
\[
 n^2\{R_n(1)-R_n(L_n^*)\}\longrightarrow4/9>0
\]
along c=1/2. Thus the disagreement concerns the second-order risk term that selects the oracle hyperparameter. All fixed positive L can share the same first-order \(1/n\) risk; no first-order efficiency loss or empirical ranking reversal is asserted.

**Why the argument fails.** Treating the other true groups as an effective residual creates a nonzero mean in the transformed noise of equations (29)–(30). That mean tends to zero, but its interaction with the group's own shrinkage bias contributes at the same \(n^{-2}\) order that determines the optimal L. It cannot be discarded merely because Lemma 20 proves it vanishes. The proof of Proposition 15 is omitted and invokes the single-block argument of Aravkin et al. (2012), Theorem 6; the recovered cited source explicitly takes p=1 and has unbiased transformed noise, so it does not justify this extension.

The displayed MSE formula on PDF page 19 also drops powers of n: direct calculation from \(z=d\beta+\epsilon\) gives numerator \(\beta^2+n^2L^2d^2(m^2+\sigma_\epsilon^2)-2nLd m\beta\). Correcting those printed scaling errors does not resolve the counterexample, which uses the genuine risk of the estimator directly.

**Reason for rejection.** A named main contribution is the extension of the non-Bayesian MSE explanation from orthogonal regressors to correlated stochastic regressors. Proposition 15 is the result equating the ARD hyperparameter limit to a weighted frequentist oracle in that extension, and this equivalence is false already in a two-dimensional, well-conditioned model. Correcting the oracle to depend on nuisance signal and correlation removes its claimed agreement with ARD's block-energy limit. Changing a scalar group's positive weight cannot restore it. Restricting the result to asymptotically orthogonal regressors or replacing fixed-truth risk with a prior-averaged criterion withdraws the stated central scope. This invalidates a central theoretical explanation of the paper as written, even though the algorithms, orthogonal results and some empirical advantages may remain useful.

**Discovery method.** Tracing the general-regressor MSE reduction raised the question of whether a vanishing but biased transformed residual could be ignored when optimizing shrinkage. A scalar-group example removes ambiguity about the proposed weighting and exposed the nuisance-bias interaction.

**Verification method.** Read the full original paper and Appendix A; rechecked rendered original definitions, Proposition 15 and discussion on PDF pages 18–20. Derived exact bias and covariance from the original posterior-mean formula, proved global minimality by differentiation, and verified the finite optimizer and limit in SymPy. Independent finite-matrix covariance-plus-bias calculations at five sample sizes agree. Inspected the cited 2012 source, pages 1–4 including rendered page 3, for any resolving assumption. A second reviewer independently reread relevant original pages and derived the same finite optimizer and risk-gap limit; this was bounded QA, not a substitute for the full-paper review.

**Confidence.** High mathematical confidence and moderate-to-high rejection confidence. The counterexample satisfies the stated stochastic-design, fixed-truth and nuisance-hyperparameter conditions. The exact conditional-risk calculation is independent of extraction and of the printed MSE scaling typo. The conclusion is carefully limited to the false central oracle-limit equivalence.

Reproducible evidence is stored in unpublished audit files: `mse-certificate.py`, `mse-certificate-results.json`, `candidate.md`, full coverage notes, independent bounded QA, and the cited source.

\[ d_{1,n}^2=\frac1nG_1^\top(I+G_2G_2^\top)^{-1}G_1 =\frac{n(1-c^2)+1}{n+1}>0, \]
so the weighted scalar-group risk is simply the positive L-independent factor \(d_{1,n}^4\) times (A).

Set \(z=u/L\). Differentiating \([V+(z-h)^2]/(z+K)^2\) gives a derivative whose sign is the sign of

\[ (z-h)(K+h)-V. \]
For c>0, it has exactly one positive zero, yielding the unique global minimizer
\[ L_n^*=\frac{u(K+h)}{h(K+h)+V} \longrightarrow\frac1{1+c_n}\longrightarrow\frac23. \]
This contradicts Proposition 15's asserted limit \(\bar\theta_1^2/k_1=1\). At c=1/2 the finite-n optimizer simplifies to
\[ L_n^*=\frac{6n^2+18n+12}{9n^2+18n+8}. \]

along c=1/2. Thus the disagreement concerns the second-order risk term that selects the oracle hyperparameter. All fixed positive L can share the same first-order \(1/n\) risk; no first-order efficiency loss or empirical ranking reversal is asserted.

It cannot be discarded merely because Lemma 20 proves it vanishes. The proof of Proposition 15 is omitted and invokes the single-block argument of Aravkin et al. Reason for rejection.

A named main contribution is the extension of the non-Bayesian MSE explanation from orthogonal regressors to correlated stochastic regressors. Proposition 15 is the result equating the ARD hyperparameter limit to a weighted frequentist oracle in that extension, and this equivalence is false already in a two-dimensional, well-conditioned model. Correcting the oracle to depend on nuisance signal and correlation removes its claimed agreement with ARD's block-energy limit. Changing a scalar group's positive weight cannot restore it. Restricting the result to asymptotically orthogonal regressors or replacing fixed-truth risk with a prior-averaged criterion withdraws the stated central scope. This invalidates a central theoretical explanation of the paper as written, even though the algorithms, orthogonal results and some empirical advantages may remain useful.

Discovery method.

Tracing the general-regressor MSE reduction raised the question of whether a vanishing but biased transformed residual could be ignored when optimizing shrinkage. A scalar-group example removes ambiguity about the proposed weighting and exposed the nuisance-bias interaction.

Read the full original paper and Appendix A; rechecked rendered original definitions, Proposition 15 and discussion on PDF pages 18–20. Independent finite-matrix covariance-plus-bias calculations at five sample sizes agree. Inspected the cited 2012 source, pages 1–4 including rendered page 3, for any resolving assumption. A second reviewer independently reread relevant original pages and derived the same finite optimizer and risk-gap limit; this was bounded QA, not a substitute for the full-paper review.

Confidence.

High mathematical confidence and moderate-to-high rejection confidence. The counterexample satisfies the stated stochastic-design, fixed-truth and nuisance-hyperparameter conditions. The exact conditional-risk calculation is independent of extraction and of the printed MSE scaling typo. The conclusion is carefully limited to the false central oracle-limit equivalence.

Reproducible evidence is stored in unpublished audit files: mse-certificate.py, mse-certificate-results.json, candidate.md, full coverage notes, independent bounded QA, and the cited source.

findings.title: The main general-prior consistency theorem is false
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2014__accepted__v15-archer14a-01 — The main general-prior consistency theorem is false
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Original PDF 14, Section 5, Theorem 4; its proof in Appendix C, original PDF 28–33, especially the omitted positive pole in the displayed bound onPDF 30 and the uniform-integral assertion onPDF 29. The abstractPDF 1 and conclusionPDF 18 advertise the consistency contribution.

**Claim.** For any proper or bounded improper hyperprior \(p(d,\alpha)\), a fixed countably infinite discrete distribution \(\pi\) satisfying \(K_N=o_p(N^{1-1/C})\) for some \(C>0\) has
\[
\left|E[H\mid X_N]-\widehat H_{\rm plugin}(X_N)\right|\longrightarrow_p0.
\]
Here \(K_N\) is the number of occupied species. The theorem imposes no further regularity on the occupied-species frequencies or near-\(d=1\) behavior of a proper prior.

**Error and evidence.** The following is one fixed bounded proper prior and one fixed countably infinite, finite-entropy distribution satisfying the stated occupancy assumption. The estimator instead diverges away from the plug-in estimate along a deterministic sample-size subsequence, with probability tending to 1.

### 1. Fixed prior and fixed true distribution

Take independent uniform \(\alpha\in[1,2]\) and \(d\in[0,1)\). This is a bounded probability density on a rectangle of area1. All parameters are in the paper's valid Pitman–Yor domain.

Define recursively
\[
R_j=1+\sum_{i<j}M_i,\qquad L_j=10R_j^2+j,\qquad
M_j=2^{4L_j},\quad N_j=2^{3L_j},\quad \tau_j=2^{-j-L_j}.
\]
Give each of the \(M_j\) distinct atoms in block\(j\) probability \(\tau_j/M_j=2^{-j-5L_j}\), and put the remaining probability on one head atom. This specifies **one fixed distribution**, independently of sample size; \(N_j\) only selects a subsequence of iid sample sizes.

Since \(L_j\ge j+10\), \(\sum_j\tau_j\le1/3072\). All probabilities are positive and sum to 1. Its entropy is finite: the head contribution is at most \(1/3072\), and
\[
\sum_j\tau_j\log(M_j/\tau_j)
\le 2^{-10}\log2\sum_{j\ge1}4^{-j}(6j+50)
=\frac{58\log2}{3072}.
\]
Thus \(H(\pi)<0.014\)nats. The sorted probabilities even have an \(O(i^{-5/4})\) envelope: cumulative block size is at most \(2M_j\), while its individual probabilities are at most \(M_j^{-5/4}\).

For every sample size,
\[
E K_N\le1+\sum_j\min(M_j,N\tau_j)
\le1+N^{4/5}\sum_j2^{-4j/5},
\]
using \(\min(a,b)\le a^{1/5}b^{4/5}\). Markov's inequality therefore gives \(K_N=o_p(N^{0.9})\), exactly the theorem's assumption with \(C=10\).

### 2. High-probability sample profiles

At \(N=N_j\), the block-\(j\) observation count \(S_j\) has mean
\(\lambda_j=N_j\tau_j=2^{2L_j-j}\). With probability tending to 1:

- \(\lambda_j/2\le S_j\le2\lambda_j\), by Chebyshev, with failure probability at most \(4/\lambda_j\).
- Every block-\(j\) observation is a singleton. The probability of any within-block collision is at most \(\binom{N_j}{2}\tau_j^2/M_j\le4^{-j}/2\).
- No later block is observed. Its probability is at most \(N_j\sum_{i>j}\tau_i\le2^{3L_j-j-L_{j+1}}\to 0\), because \(L_{j+1}\ge10\,2^{8L_j}\).
- The head is observed at least twice, since its fixed probability is positive.

Call this event \(E_j\). On it, \(K\ge\lambda_j/2\), and the number \(r\) of species observed at least twice satisfies \(1\le r\le R_j\). Also \(K\le2\lambda_j+R_j\ll N_j\), so the paper's collision-based finiteness condition holds eventually.

### 3. Exact posterior bound

This is a deterministic calculation for any positive integer counts \(n_1,\ldots,n_K\), total \(N\), with \(r\) repeated species. Conditional on any \(\alpha\in[1,2]\), write \(\delta=1-d\). Equation 17 makes its posterior density proportional to \(\delta^rF_\alpha(\delta)\), where
\[
F_\alpha(\delta)=
\prod_{\ell=1}^{K-1}[\alpha+\ell(1-\delta)]
\prod_{i:n_i\ge2}\prod_{q=2}^{n_i-1}(q-1+\delta).
\]
Empty products equal1, and \(F_\alpha(0)>0\). The remaining gamma factors are independent of\(\delta\) and cancel in its conditional density.

For \(0<\delta\le1/2\), \(\log(1-u\delta)\ge-2\delta\) for \(0\le u\le1\), giving
\[
F_\alpha(\delta)\ge F_\alpha(0)e^{-2K\delta}.
\]
For all \(0<\delta<1\), the inequalities \(\log(1-u\delta)\le-u\delta\) and \(\log(1+v)\le v\) give
\[
F_\alpha(\delta)\le F_\alpha(0)e^{-a\delta},\qquad
 a=K-1-2H_{K-1}-rH_{N-2},
\]
where \(H_m\) denotes a harmonic number. The coefficient2 uses \(\alpha\le2\); each repeated species contributes at most \(H_{N-2}\) to the second product's logarithmic derivative.

If \(a\ge K/2\) and \(K\ge2r\), gamma integrals give the **uniform-in-\(\alpha\)** bound
\[
\begin{aligned}
E[1/\delta\mid\alpha,X]
&=\frac{\int_0^1\delta^{r-1}F_\alpha(\delta)\,d\delta}
        {\int_0^1\delta^rF_\alpha(\delta)\,d\delta}\\
&\ge\frac{\Gamma(r)/[2(2K)^r]}
              {\Gamma(r+1)(2/K)^{r+1}}
 =\frac{K}{4r4^r}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For the numerator, integrate only to \(1/2\), substitute \(u=2K\delta\), and use \(P\{\mathrm{Gamma}(r,1)\le K\}\ge1-r/K\ge1/2\). For the denominator, extend the upper exponential envelope to infinity.

The two conditions hold on \(E_j\) eventually: \(r\le R_j\), \(\log K\le\log N_j=3L_j\log2\), and \(K\ge2^{2L_j-j-1}\), whereas the adverse harmonic terms are only \(O(R_j^3)\). Here\(j\le R_j\) and\(L_j\le11R_j^2\).

### 4. The actual entropy estimate diverges

AppendixA's posterior decomposition has unseen mass with mean \((\alpha+Kd)/(N+\alpha)\), independent of normalized unseen weights following \(\mathrm{PY}(d,\alpha+Kd)\). Their expected entropy is
\[
\psi(\alpha+Kd+1)-\psi(\delta)\ge1/\delta,
\]
because \(\alpha+Kd+1\ge2\ge1+\delta\) and \(\psi(\delta)=\psi(1+\delta)-1/\delta\). All other entropy contributions are nonnegative. Thus
\[
E[H\mid\alpha,X]\ge\frac{K}{N+2}
\{E[1/\delta\mid\alpha,X]-1\}.
\]
Uniformity in\(\alpha\) lets us average this over its exact posterior. On \(E_j\),
\[
E[H\mid X_{N_j}]
\ge\frac{K^2}{4(N_j+2)r4^r}-\frac{K}{N_j+2}
\ge\frac{2^{L_j-2j}}{32R_j4^{R_j}}-1.
\]
This last bound grows much faster than \(\log N_j=3L_j\log2\). But \(\widehat H_{\rm plugin}\le\log N_j\) for every dataset. Consequently
\[
E[H\mid X_{N_j}]-\widehat H_{\rm plugin}(X_{N_j})\longrightarrow_p+\infty,
\]
contradicting Theorem 4's convergence to 0. Every finite-stage posterior integral in this argument is finite; this is an asymptotic inconsistency, not an undefined-posterior endpoint.

**Connection to the failed proof.** PDF 30 asserts \(E[H\mid\alpha,d,X]\le\psi(N+\alpha+1)\), dropping the positive unbounded term \(-(\alpha+Kd)\psi(1-d)/(N+\alpha)\). For counts\((2,2)\), \(\alpha=1,d=.99\), the exact conditional mean is61.4670031263, versus the asserted upper bound1.70611766843. PDF 29's pointwise integrability does not supply uniform posterior control. The counterexample demonstrates why that missing control matters: many singleton species and relatively few repeatedly seen species drive \(d\) too close to 1 and produce a large inferred unseen-tail entropy.

**Reason for rejection.** Asymptotic consistency for a broad class is an expressly advertised principal theoretical contribution. The central theorem is false under its own bounded proper prior and occupancy assumptions, for a fixed finite-entropy distribution with a polynomial tail envelope. The failure is unbounded and occurs with probability approaching1 along a subsequence. Fixing a sign, numerical constant or displayed envelope does not restore the stated guarantee. A revised result needs additional restrictions on the repeat-species profile or the hyperprior's behavior near\(d=1\), plus different posterior analysis. Restricting the prior away from\(d=1\) withdraws the theorem's advertised scope and does not cover all stated full-domain mixtures. This loss warrants rejection as written even though the conditional moment formulas and estimator construction can survive.

**Discovery method.** Traced the consistency proof after noticing its omitted positive pole, then investigated whether the likelihood factors supplied the missing uniform bound. The distinction between the number of occupied species and the number seen repeatedly led to the separated-block construction.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the original theorem, EPPF, posterior decomposition and proof in the PDF, including rendered 14/27/29/30/33. Derived the exact EPPF factorization and both deterministic exponential bounds; checked every theorem assumption for one fixed distribution and prior. Independent audit by the root reviewer reproduced the construction and inequalities; `root-consistency-qa.md` and `root-consistency-qa.json` retain that bounded assessment. Fresh numerical checks of 500 factor envelopes and 5 finite profiles at 3 alpha values and 3 integration cutoffs support the derivation; the asymptotic contradiction rests on the exact inequalities above, not those quadratures.

 For example, the fresh profile with 9000 observations of one species plus 1000 singletons has plug-in entropy 1.0158585; exact one-dimensional conditional-alpha posterior quadrature yields entropy 99.29–99.75 foralpha 1–2. This is a supporting finite profile, not a replacement for the fixed-distribution asymptotic certificate.

**Confidence: High.** Exact analytic counterexample satisfies the hyperprior, iid fixed countably infinite distribution and occupancy assumptions. Independent derivation agrees. No claim is made that the paper's specific default\(q(\gamma)\) mixture is inconsistent, or that its finite-sample comparisons are falsified; the reported issue is the single general-prior consistency theorem and its dependent broad claim.

sections.title: What may be wrong
sections.html: A permitted bounded proper prior can retain too much posterior mass near a singularity. The posterior entropy estimate then diverges along a sample-size sequence, despite the stated occupancy condition.
sections.markdown: A permitted bounded proper prior can retain too much posterior mass near a singularity. The posterior entropy estimate then diverges along a sample-size sequence, despite the stated occupancy condition.

sections.title: Evidence in brief
sections.html:
The audit fixes a uniform prior on α in [1,2] and d in [0,1), together with one countably infinite block distribution. The distribution has finite entropy and controlled expected occupancy:

\[ H(\pi)<0.014,\qquad \mathbb E[K_N]=O(N^{0.8}). \]

findings.title: The weak-neighborhood recovery theorem fails on an exact finite instance
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2014__accepted__v15-balcan14a-01 — The weak-neighborhood recovery theorem fails on an exact finite instance
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Original PDF20, Section4.2, Theorem4 (printed4030); assumptions in Property5 on PDF19; Algorithm1 on PDF9. The invalid purity/laminarity and good-proportion steps are Lemma5 on PDF21 and Lemma7 on PDF22; Lemma8 and the theorem rely on them. Original PDF5 defines success using any pruning, rather than only a horizontal cut.

**Claim.** If a symmetric similarity function satisfies the weak `(alpha,beta,nu)` good-neighborhood property with `beta>=7/8`, Algorithm1 outputs a hierarchy having a pruning with error at most `nu`. Property5 allows each nonbad point a local set `A_p` inside its target cluster, containing the point and larger than `6(alpha+nu)n`. Every member has at most `alpha*n` outsiders among its `|A_p|` nearest neighbors; every such local set must contain at least a `beta` fraction of globally good points. A globally good point has at most `alpha*n` outsiders among its target-cluster-size nearest neighbors after bad points are removed.

**Error and evidence.** The following symmetric, rational, tie-free112point instance satisfies these assumptions, including the stronger universal interpretation of “any such subset,” but neither target cluster is a node of the output hierarchy.

Number points `0,...,111`. Let `L_h={28h,...,28h+27}`, `h=0,1,2,3`. In each local group, `g_(h,i)=28h+i` are14core points and `b_(h,i)=28h+14+i` are14boundary points, for `i=0,...,13`. The two target clusters are

```
C0 = L0 union L1,   C1 = L2 union L3,
n = 112,   alpha = 1/112,   nu = 0,   beta = 7/8,   B = empty.
```

Define a symmetric base similarity with diagonal1 and the following off-diagonal values:

| Pair | Base similarity |
|---|---:|
| Two cores in the same `L_h` | `.99 − .0001*d(i,j)`, where `d=min(|i−j|,14−|i−j|)` |
| `g_(h,i),b_(h,j)` | `.951` if `i=j`, otherwise `.95` |
| Two boundaries in the same `L_h` | `.1` |
| Different local groups in the same target cluster | `.8` |
| Boundaries in different target clusters | `.9` |
| Any remaining pair in different target clusters | `.01` |

For distinct point indices `p,q`, add `10^(-9)*(224−p−q)` to the base value. Keep the diagonal1. This perturbation is symmetric, keeps all entries in `[0,1]`, preserves every ordering between different base levels and resolves every tie within a row in ascending point-index order. All similarities are exact integers divided by `10^10`; no PSD or metric assumption is required by the paper.

Nearest-neighbor lists include the query point. This agrees with the paper's target-size convention and iteration up to `t=n`, and is explicit in the recovered author source (`similarity.NuNPlus1Affinity` comments that nearest neighbors always contain self; RMNL keeps self scores and initializes graph diagonals to1). The separate convention about self-loops in `F_t` does not affect the failure: both were checked independently.

*Checking the assumptions.* Every core's first56neighbors are exactly its own target cluster, so all56cores are globally good. Every boundary has its self and14local cores first, followed by28boundaries of the other target cluster; it has28outsiders among its first56neighbors and is not globally good.

For each boundary point, choose its local witness to be all14cores in its local group together with that boundary. For a core, choose the14local cores together with the group's first boundary. Each witness has15points, exceeding `6(alpha+nu)n=6`. A boundary in a witness has zero outsiders among its first15neighbors. A core has at most one outsider: its own favored boundary may be missing. Good-point fraction is `14/15>7/8`.

The second bullet of Property5 also holds for **every** eligible local set `A` within a target cluster, rather than just these witnesses. Write `q=|A|>6`:

1. If `A` contains a boundary and `q>=17`, that boundary already has two foreign-target points among its first17neighbors. Thus `A` is not locally good. Consequently any locally good set containing a boundary has `7<=q<=16`.
2. For these sizes, all same-target points in a member's first `q` neighbors belong to that member's own local group. Local goodness therefore requires at least `q−1` members of `A` in that group. Two different local groups cannot both be represented, since `2(q−1)>q`.
3. Inside one local group, write `c` for the number of cores and `b` for boundaries in `A`. A boundary's first `q` neighbors contain at most `c+1` members of `A`, implying `b<=2`.
4. If `b=1` and `c/(c+1)<7/8`, the only possibility is `c=6,q=7`. For each of these six cores, all six selected cores would have to lie in its first7neighbors. Those first7neighbors are the core itself and its six neighbors at cyclic distance at most3. There is no six-clique in the third power of the14cycle (maximum clique size4). This can also be checked by all `choose(14,6)=3003` core subsets.
5. If `b=2,c<=12`, a selected core's first `q=c+2<=14` neighbors are all cores. At least two are outside `A`, so `A` is not locally good. If `b=2,c=13,q=15`, the missing core already uses the one permitted outsider; every selected core would then need its distinct favored boundary in `A`, impossible with only two boundaries. Finally `c=14,b=2` has good fraction exactly `7/8`.

Core-only sets have good fraction1. This covers every case and proves the universal condition. A separate exhaustive check examined5,596,136potential below-beta local subsets and found none valid.

*Running the published algorithm.* Here `eta=(alpha+nu)n=1`, so Algorithm1 starts at `t=7`. Both independent implementations give:

| Threshold | Actual merge/result |
|---|---|
| `t=7` | The singleton `H_t` components are precisely `L0,L1,L2,L3`; each28point group is merged. |
| `8<=t<=109` | No further merge. Every across-target blob-pair median is0; every same-target median is at most14, failing the strict `>(28+28)/4=14` test. |
| `t=110` | All six blob pairs pass simultaneously; Step4 merges the whole connected component into the112point root. |

All intermediate thresholds were checked, not just `t=|C_i|`. For example, at `t=56` the same-target median equals14 exactly, so it fails the strict test. At `t=110`, any two110element subsets of112points intersect in at least108=`t−2`; hence `F_t` is complete, and the root merge is unavoidable.

The hierarchy consists of singleton leaves, the four local-group nodes, and the root. Neither56point target cluster occurs. In particular there is no two-node pruning at all: selecting the root gives one node, whereas any pruning below it must cover its four children. Allowing different depths does not help. Thus the promised zero-error pruning does not exist.

The proof fails for the same structural reason. Each28point local-group blob is fully formed, since all its selected15point witnesses lie inside it, yet only14/28of its points are globally good. This directly contradicts Lemma7's claimed fraction at least7/8. Overlapping witnesses repeatedly reuse the same cores; their individual good fractions do not imply that their union has that fraction. Lemma5's claimed local-set purity cannot hold simultaneously for these overlapping, nonnested witnesses, and its use to deduce laminarity is invalid.

**Reason for rejection.** Section4's treatment of boundary points is an expressly advertised central extension beyond the stronger good-neighborhood model (introduction PDF3 and Section4 PDF16–24). Its main recovery theorem is false under its own assumptions, even without adversarial bad points, metric complications or ties. The false conclusion prevents repairing the proof by filling in a line. Adding a laminar/disjoint witness-cover assumption would change the stated weak-neighborhood class and remove the reuse-of-cores cases it presently permits; changing the algorithm needs a new correctness argument. Merely making each multiway merge binary does not generally fix the problem: the recovered practical implementation fails on a relabeling of the same instance, as described below. With this central robustness result withdrawn, the paper as written warrants reject. The stronger Theorem1 and historical benchmark ordering are not claimed false by this issue.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the weak-property induction, noticed that Lemma5/7 would force arbitrary overlapping local witnesses to be laminar. First constructed an auxiliary overlapping-witness example, then investigated whether repeatedly reused good cores could make a fully formed blob predominantly boundary points. This led to the112point construction and the actual theorem counterexample.

**Verification method.** Rechecked original definitions, Algorithm1 and Theorem4, including full rendered PDF9/19/20/21/22. Built two separate implementations: NumPy graph products, and exact integer similarities with Python-set intersections and integer doubled-median comparisons. Both checked every threshold7through110 and both `F_t` self-loop conventions. Verified all112witnesses, all global good/boundary counts, the universal local-set argument and exhaustive below-beta candidates. An independent reviewer rebuilt the rational matrix, checked the assumptions and every threshold, and obtained the same failure.

As an additional implementation control, ran the authentic author-linked MATLAB core unchanged in Octave using a matrix wrapper and an explicitly documented undirected connected-components compatibility function. Practical Algorithm3 recovers the targets for the natural ordering `L0,L1,L2,L3`, a favorable result retained in the evidence. Permuting the tie-free instance to `L0,L2,L1,L3` makes its sole two-cluster pruning have56/112misclassified points under either label permutation. This is the same underlying weak-property failure, not a second issue. The practical code also achieved best error7/178on a ten-parameter Wine control, consistent with the paper's approximate.04error; no full historical benchmark rerun or empirical-comparison reversal is claimed.

- `weak-candidate-control.py/.json/.log`: explicit witnesses,5,596,136subset checks and matrix-product Algorithm1.
- `exact-independent-control.py/.json/.log` and `exact-K-scaled.csv`: tie-free exact rational matrix, independent set implementation, both self-loop conventions.
- `all-threshold-median-control.json`: every blob-pair median for thresholds8through109.
- `root-bounded-qa.py/.json/.md` and `root-bounded-qa-output.txt`: independent bounded review and reconstruction.
- `source-provenance.json`, `native-run_controls.m`, `native-graphconncomp.m`, `native-auditSimilarity.m`, `native-controls.log`, `native-run_permuted.m`, `native-permuted.log`, `native-permuted-results.txt`: source provenance and favorable/adverse native controls.
- `whole-paper-notes.md`: remaining claim checks and limits, including unavailable full historical experiment drivers.

Run the two Python controls with NumPy available; the integer set control and generated matrix remove floating comparison ambiguity. An initial JSON serialization failure occurred after mathematical assertions passed, was corrected without changing the construction and was rerun successfully.

**Confidence: High.** Every assumption is verified, the counterexample is finite and rational with distinct row scores, both independent implementations and independent reviewer reproduce the exact hierarchy, and the theorem fails as a statement about any pruning. The finding does not depend on unavailable experimental artifacts or on inferring that a proof gap makes a theorem false.

findings.title: Uniform node selection makes the central spectral estimator inconsistent
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2014__accepted__v15-cohen14a__I01 — Uniform node selection makes the central spectral estimator inconsistent
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem 6 and equations (14)–(20), PDF page 19 / journal page 2417; Theorem 8, PDF page 22 / journal page 2420. The sampling rule is stated on PDF pages 18 and 20 / journal pages 2416 and 2418. Figure 7, PDF page 23, and Figure 8, PDF page 24, specify the empirical estimator. The first false population factorization is in Appendix A.2, PDF page 29 / journal page 2427; related independence steps occur in A.4–A.5, PDF pages 31–32. These are two of the three central results advertised in the abstract and introduction, PDF pages 1–2.

**Claim.** Draw iid full trees from the L-PCFG and choose one node uniformly from each tree. Under Conditions 1 and 2 (full-rank conditional inside/outside feature means, positive latent-state weights and invertible projected means), Theorem 6 identifies the resulting observable moments with linearly transformed true grammar parameters. Theorem 8 asserts that, for bounded features and positive minimum binary-rule probability \(\gamma\), increasing the stated finite sample counts makes
\[
 \sum_{t\in\mathcal T(a,N)}|\widehat p(t)-p(t)|\leq\epsilon
\]
with probability at least \(1-\delta\). Here \(N\) is the number of binary rules in a target tree.

**Error and evidence.** Choosing a uniform node *after* drawing the tree multiplies the joint probability of a particular tree/node pair by the inverse total tree size. That weight depends on both the inside and outside trees. It changes rule probabilities and invalidates the PCFG independence factorization used in Appendix A.2. This remains true with no latent ambiguity.

Consider this fully positive, finite-mean example:

- One hidden state, one word \(x\), one interminal \(S\), and one preterminal \(P\); the root is always \(S\).
- \(P\to x\) has probability one.
- The four possible binary rules from \(S\) have probabilities
\[
 t(S\to PP)=\tfrac12,\qquad
 t(S\to SP)=t(S\to PS)=\tfrac15,\qquad
 t(S\to SS)=\tfrac1{10}.
\]
- Take the scalar features and projections \(\phi=\psi=U^a=V^a=1\) for both labels.

All rule probabilities are normalized. The expected number of \(S\) children is \(2/5+2/10=3/5<1\), so the grammar generates finite trees almost surely and has expected total tree size six. Every allowed binary rule is strictly positive, with \(\gamma=1/10\). Every conditional inside/outside mean, projected mean and correlation matrix equals the scalar one. Thus all rank/invertibility assumptions hold, all feature norms are one, and the theorem's \(\sigma=\xi=1\). No structural-zero rule, singular feature, improper grammar, infinite mean or empirical misspecification is used in this counterexample.

Let \(K\geq1\) be the number of \(S\) nodes; the total number of rule nodes is \(2K+1\). Write \(a=1/2\), \(r=2/5\), \(d=1/10\), and let \(F(z)=\mathbb E[z^K]\). The branching recursion gives
\[
 F(z)=z\{a+rF(z)+dF(z)^2\},\qquad
 D(z)=1-z\{r+2dF(z)\}>0.
\]
Marking the number \(L\) of occurrences of \(S\to PP\) gives
\[
 \mathbb E[Lz^K]=a\,\partial_aF(z)=\frac{az}{D(z)},\qquad
 \mathbb E[Kz^K]=zF'(z)=\frac{F(z)}{D(z)}.
\]
The derivative in \(a\) is a formal marking derivative of tree weights, with the other rule weights fixed. Using \(1/(2K+1)=\int_0^1x^{2K}\,dx\), define
\[
 A=\mathbb E\frac{K}{2K+1}
   =\int_0^1\frac{F(x^2)}{D(x^2)}\,dx,
 \qquad
 B=\mathbb E\frac{L}{2K+1}
   =a\int_0^1\frac{x^2}{D(x^2)}\,dx.
\]
Under the paper's sampler, \(A\) is the probability that the selected label is \(S\), and \(B\) is the probability that its rule is \(S\to PP\). Since all features equal one, the estimator in Figure 7 converges exactly to the conditional frequency \(B/A\), while \(\widehat\Sigma^S=1\), the lexical parameter is one, and the root parameter is one whenever their counts are nonzero.

The bias has an exact lower bound. Because \(\Pr(K=1)=a\),
\[
 F(z)\leq az+(1-a)z^2\quad(0\leq z\leq1),
 \qquad 0<D(z)\leq1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 B-aA
 =a\int_0^1\frac{x^2-F(x^2)}{D(x^2)}\,dx
 \geq a(1-a)\int_0^1(x^2-x^4)\,dx
 =\frac1{30}.
\]
Also \(A<1/2\), because \(K/(2K+1)<1/2\). Hence
\[
 \frac BA-a>\frac1{15}.
\]

\]
The exact inequality, rather than this numerical calculation, proves the contradiction.

For \(N=1\), \(\mathcal T(S,1)\) contains precisely this short tree. Choose, for example, \(\epsilon=1/30\), \(\delta=1/10\). The label and root sampling masses are positive, so every required \(N_a,M_a,R\) tends to infinity linearly in the two independent iid sample sizes. For any fixed proposed constants in Theorem 8, its finite thresholds are eventually satisfied with probability tending to one. By the iid law of large numbers, the error nevertheless exceeds \(\epsilon\) with probability tending to one. The estimator is inconsistent, not merely slower than the displayed rate. Theorem 6 already fails at the population level because its scalar \(C^{S\to PP}\) is \(B/A\), whereas its required true parameter is \(a=1/2\).

For an additional exact control, the critical but proper grammar with all four binary probabilities \(1/4\) gives \(F(z)=(1-\sqrt{1-z})/(1+\sqrt{1-z})\), \(A=(4-\pi)/2\), \(B=\pi/16\), and the false limit \(\pi/[8(4-\pi)]\approx0.4574740458\) instead of \(1/4\). **Reason for rejection.** The observable representation and PAC-style consistent estimator are two named central contributions. Both fail under the paper's actual sampling procedure, even for an elementary ordinary PCFG satisfying every substantive nondegeneracy and boundedness assumption. Unlimited data do not remove the bias, so the claimed advantage of a statistically consistent spectral estimator is unsupported as written.

The practical suggestion to pool all nodes on PDF page 22 does not establish the stated theorem. Pooling nodes globally changes the target law and produces dependent observations; its consistency and concentration need a replacement analysis. Averaging each tree's nodes with weight inverse tree size is instead the actual Rao–Blackwellization of the printed sampler and retains this bias. Importance weighting sampled tuples by tree size changes the estimator and introduces unbounded weights for permissible models.

A different iid sampler can salvage the spectral idea: independently choose a finite binary node address with probability \(1/(2\cdot4^{\text{depth}})\) and discard absent addresses. This avoids inside-dependent selection and accepts at least half the trees. It changes the sampling law and the rank/singular-value assumptions, however. For a concrete check, use two equally probable trees generated by \(S\to PP\) or \(S\to IP\), with \(I\to PP\), \(P\to x\), and \(\phi=1\). Set the outside feature for a \(P\) foot to \(3/4\) in a short-tree context and \(-1\) in a long-tree context, and to one for the other labels. Thus the replacement theorem's premises do not follow from the original ones, even for bounded-size trees and the same fixed features. These are possible new analyses/algorithms, not corrections validating the published central guarantee. The valid tensor algebra and separate empirical parsing results remain useful, but do not establish the two false central theorems.

I first checked a two-tree example, then constructed a fully positive grammar to ensure that the finite sample-complexity theorem was genuinely contradicted.

**Verification method.** I rechecked the full PDF and both appendices, and inspected original rendered pages for the sampler, theorem, estimator and failed proof steps. I derived the branching generating function and the exact lower bound above, checked the formulas by 70-digit quadrature, and ran a fresh seeded control on 60,000 finite-mean trees. It gave 0.67175 for the printed uniform-node estimator, versus 0.50142 for the alternative address sampler and 0.50131 for pooled counts, with true probability 0.5. Exact fractions verify the change in rank premises. Two additional bounded reviews independently checked original sampling/theorem pages and the exact counterexamples; these were not substitutes for the full-paper review. Independent tensor/gauge controls on 60 random two-state models confirmed the unaffected algebra. These are fresh checks, not reruns of the historical parser. Original author-linked companion text and a later author-associated implementation explicitly use all-node counts; their reported F1/timing results are not disproved.

Moderate-to-high in the rejection assessment: the failure directly affects two advertised central results, and the concrete sampling repairs require new laws/premises or a new dependence analysis. findings.title: Most of the new off-policy comparison uses the behavior-policy Bellman error
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2014__accepted__v15-dann14a-I01 — Most of the new off-policy comparison uses the behavior-policy Bellman error
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF 37 (printed 845), Section 2.4.2 definition of the off-policy objective; PDF 46–47 (854–855), Section 3.1.7 hyperparameter selection and evaluation; PDF 59–60 (867–868), Message 8, Table 8 and Figure 26a; PDF 64 (872), central contribution summary. In the paper-linked implementation, commit `7ad9c0e2485a86897a11e8c3c2bba2460efe3cd7` dated 2013-11-04: `task.py`576–621 (discrete Bellman operator/MSBE/MSPBE),805–855 and904–919 (LQR Bellman operator/MSBE/MSPBE),473–498 (criterion callback); `experiments/gridsearch.py`99–110 and `experiments/__init__.py`93–101.

**Claim.** Off-policy evaluation estimates the value of the target policy pi_G from behavior-policy pi_B trajectories. The paper explicitly defines its off-policy projected Bellman error using the target Bellman operator T_G and a projection/norm under the behavior-state distribution D_B. Section 3.1.7 says the algorithms are tuned against MSBE or MSPBE and evaluated with those costs. The new transition-reweighted LSTD/LSPE methods are then compared to standard reweighting across five off-policy tasks in Table 8, supporting the central practical recommendation in Message 8 and the conclusion. This requires the reported errors and parameter selection to use T_G, despite observations being generated under pi_B.

**Error and evidence.** The paper-linked source instead evaluates the behavior-policy Bellman operator T_B in the discrete and LQR task classes. `MSBE` and `MSPBE` call `bellman_operator` without the policy argument, whose default is behavior. The four affected benchmark drivers (tasks 4,6,8,12) all select the ordinary RMSPBE/RMSBE callbacks; they do not override these functions or request the target operator. Grid search forwards the same callbacks, so the error affects hyperparameter selection as well as reported curves and aggregate scores. In the discrete task, R/P are moreover cached without a policy key; no driver or target-value routine initializes those caches to the target first. The LQR target-value routine has separate target caches and does not change the default behavior operator. The complete missed-resolution/call-chain check is retained in unpublished audit files.

The mismatch is substantive even with full support, strictly positive stationary state probabilities, exact model expectations and perfect features. Take two states 0/1 and two actions 0/1. Action a deterministically sends either current state to state a and yields reward a. In either state let pi_B(action1)=1/100, pi_G(action1)=99/100; both policies choose the other action with the complementary positive probability. Both chains are irreducible and aperiodic. Let gamma=9/10 and Phi=I_2, so projection is the identity under either positive state distribution and both values are represented exactly. Then

    V_G=(99/10,99/10),       V_B=(1/10,1/10).
    V_G - T_G V_G = 0,
    V_G - T_B V_G = (49/50,49/50),
    V_B - T_B V_B = 0,
    V_B - T_G V_B = (-49/50,-49/50).

Thus true target MSBE and MSPBE are 0 at V_G, while the implemented criteria are 2401/2500=.9604; they are 0 at the wrong behavior value V_B, whose true target errors are .9604. The native Python2 implementation reproduces these quantities in `native-source-checks.json`; this is an exact target substitution, rather than sampling uncertainty or a weighting convention.

A further controlled run uses the actual native task 6 model, features, methods and selected driver parameters, with five paired seeds and 30000 behavior transitions per seed. Only the evaluation operator is changed to target. Mean summedRMSPBE over 100 evaluation times changes from 24.4863 to 24.6772 for LSPE,6.16966 to 6.24472 for LSPE-TO,32.0417 to 32.0924 for LSTD, and6.15444 to 6.22991 for LSTD-TO. This confirms the real benchmark evaluates different costs. The TO ranking survives this bounded correction; it is not evidence that TO never helps. These five trials are not a reproduction of the historical 50-trial results or a rerun of the hyperparameter search.

**Reason for rejection.** The new practical off-policy comparison and comprehensive systematic evaluation are explicit central contributions. Four of the five Table 8 rows, including one of the two main Figure26 illustrations, were selected/scored by an operator for a different policy in the published implementation. Consequently those results do not establish the advertised target-policy comparison or its target-objective tuning. Restoring that evidence requires rerunning the affected parameter searches and evaluations and reassessing the cross-task recommendation; a code or caption correction cannot retrospectively supply it. The untouched swing-up task 10 and the bounded corrected task 6 result support a narrower TO benefit, but they do not validate the bulk published comparison. This finding warrants rejection of the empirical contribution as written while leaving open that a corrected study could support useful or even similar conclusions. It does not refute the generic survey framework or the algebraic unbiasedness of transition reweighting.

**Discovery method.** While tracing off-policy theory to the experiment/tuning code, noticed ordinary MSBE/MSPBE methods calling an operator whose default policy is behavior, contrary to the target-policy objective.

**Verification method.** Rechecked original PDF definitions, tuning procedures, Table 8/Figure26 and conclusions in rendered pages; authenticated and preserved the prepublication paper-linked repository; traced all driver/grid-search/error callback and cache paths; executed an exact two-state/perfect-feature native control; and ran five paired native task 6 trials with both the original and explicitly target-corrected evaluators. Checked the general continuous evaluator separately: it correctly takes target conditional expectations and is outside this finding.

**Confidence.** High in the concrete error; moderately high in rejection severity. The policy default, callback path and exact counterexample are direct and reproducible, and the flaw covers most of the central new-method off-policy comparison. The actual historical raw arrays/grid outputs are unavailable, so no exact reconstruction or corrected ranking reversal is claimed; the demonstrated surviving task 6 benefit and unaffected task 10 limit the conclusion to the adequacy of the paper's published central comparative evidence.

**Reproducibility and limits.** The source archive has SHA256 `3e0e499fbbb7790895a44d585315b22b8b123932de0177c51aefa27712df3dc2`; provenance and full source are under unpublished audit files. `dann-native-bootstrap.py` supplies import-only plotting/cache/parallel shims and an arithmetically identical NumPy quadratic-feature loop for the native Cython helper. Native update/dynamics equations are unchanged. `dann-native-checks.py` and `dann-cartpole-paired.py` reproduce the controls; saved JSON results distinguish them from historical reruns. No complete original 50/200-trial evaluation or parameter-grid reproduction is claimed. Independent density/sampling/LSPE scope defects are documented privately in coverage notes and are not counted again as this wrong-policy issue.

findings.title: Hyperparameter selection reuses the later test labels
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2014__accepted__v15-delgado14a-I01 — Hyperparameter selection reuses the later test labels
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF 22 (printed 3154), Section 3, validation methodology; PDF 28 (3160), paragraph below Figure 3 asserting that parameter optimization cannot bias the final result; PDF 23–31, Tables 3–5 and classifier rankings; PDF 43 (3175), general-purpose classifier recommendation.

**Claim.** The paper aims to establish reliable comparative rankings of 179 classifiers from 17 families over 121 data sets, identifying random forests as the strongest family and recommending the best implementation as a general reference. For data evaluated by cross-validation, Section 3 selects hyperparameters on one class-stratified 50/50 split of the available data, then fixes those parameters and evaluates four-fold cross-validation using the whole available data. PDF 28 explicitly reasons that tuning and testing use different data sets and the final result therefore cannot be biased by parameter optimization.

**Error and evidence.** The second-stage test labels already participated in first-stage model selection. Let S be the available data, T/V the initial tuning train/validation halves, and hhat the hyperparameter selected using the validation labels Y_V. A later test fold F is drawn from S, so it contains members of V, and often T as well. Although the numerical model weights are refitted on S minus F, the fixed hhat still depends on labels in F. Refitting at a globally chosen hyperparameter does not turn those labels into independent test data. Using the same splits for all classifiers does not remove this bias, because the selection effect depends on their search spaces and stability.

This is the procedure explicitly written in the original rendered PDF, rather than an inference from missing code. Its overlap is also visible in recovered partition artifacts. The author's original project/data/results URLs now return HTTP 410. The [maintained Torchhd dataset loader](https://github.com/hyperdimensional-computing/torchhd/blob/main/torchhd/datasets/dataset.py) explicitly identifies the original author archive. Independently, the authors' CITIUS institution hosts the four fish-oocyte data sets used in this paper, in the [fixed 2016 migration commit of fishovary](https://gitlab.citius.gal/jorge.suarez/fishovary/-/tree/4e434ce0c6fa93b7d2afe67a4c941a178613fa85). Its README identifies the same data, feature counts and originating authors/paper. All eight institutional tuning/evaluation partition files byte-match the mirror.

For the institutionally recovered Trisopterus nucleus data set, the initial validation set contains 456 of 912 examples. The four later test sets each contain 228 examples; respectively 125, 122, 114 and 120 of their examples belong to the initial validation set. Altogether 320 distinct validation examples are subsequently tested. Thus their labels influence the selected hyperparameters before being used to score the resulting classifiers. The other three authenticated data sets also have explicit overlap. The broader mirror has overlap in all 121 parsable partition pairs; that is corroboration, since byte identity of the entire mirror to the inaccessible author archive cannot be certified.

The stored test sets overlap one another as repeated holdouts, so they are not a disjoint four-fold partition. This does not resolve the tuning-label reuse, and no calculation here assumes those actual test sets are disjoint. The finding is scoped to data sets evaluated using the second-stage resampling protocol. Data sets supplied with genuinely separate, untouched external test files may avoid this defect and are not asserted to fail on that ground.

Rescaling each feature to unit variance under either sample or population conventions leaves the sign classifiers below unchanged.

An exact controlled example demonstrates that the asserted bias immunity is false, and that a common split can favor a tuned method over an equally accurate untuned one:

1. Use 12 examples with three nonconstant normalized features. The first feature is negative for six examples and positive for six; the other two are nuisance features. Assign six labels of each binary class uniformly over the 924 balanced assignments, independently of the features. Fresh labels are independent Bernoulli(1/2).
2. A classifier's only hyperparameter chooses h+(x)=1{x1>0} or h−(x)=1{x1<0}. It has no other fitted coefficients. Both candidates, and the selected candidate, have true fresh-data accuracy 1/2.
3. Use the paper's initial six/six train-validation split with three members of each class in each half. Select the direction with greater validation accuracy, breaking ties in favor of h+. Freeze that direction and evaluate four folds of three examples over all 12 examples. As the predictions have no remaining fitted coefficients, the mean fold score is exactly the full-data score of the selected direction.
4. Counting all 924 × 20² = 369,600 equally likely label/split configurations gives expected reported accuracy **269/462 = 58.2251%**, despite true accuracy **50%**. An untuned h+ reports 50% in expectation under the same splits. The artificial comparative advantage is **19/231 = 8.2251 percentage points**.

The count is reproducible without simulation. Let k be the number of positive labels among the six positive-feature examples; its assignment multiplicity is C(6,k)². If p correctly predicted positive labels and q correctly predicted negative labels enter the validation set, the split multiplicity is C(k,p)C(6−k,3−p)C(k,q)C(6−k,3−q). Select h+ if p+q≥3, yielding full-data accuracy k/6, otherwise select h−, yielding 1−k/6. Summing these weighted accuracies and dividing by 369,600 gives 269/462.

This controlled example establishes the failure mechanism and false bias claim; it is not a rerun of the paper's random forests or SVMs, and its 8.2251-point bias is not attributed to the published accuracy table.

**Reason for rejection.** The paper's central contribution is the comparative empirical evidence for its classifier rankings, optimality probabilities and general recommendation. For its cross-validated data sets, hyperparameter selection has already used labels later treated as test outcomes, so the reported scores cannot establish the claimed unbiased comparison. Classifiers have different search spaces and tuning procedures; the exact control shows that identical partitions do not make this contamination cancel between methods. Restoring the central evidence requires selecting hyperparameters inside each outer training split, or reserving a genuinely untouched test set, then rerunning and reassessing the affected comparison. A prose clarification or a new significance calculation on the same scores cannot restore independence. This warrants rejection as written without asserting that random forests would lose a correctly evaluated comparison.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the experiment protocol, noticed that the tuning split uses the available data and the subsequent evaluation again uses the whole data, contradicting the later assurance of separate tuning and testing.

**Verification method.** Read the full 49-page original, rechecked rendered methodology, bias assurance and central recommendation; inspected the recovered partition files and independently recovered the institutional historical subset; computed their exact intersections; and derived and executed the exact balanced finite selection-bias control. No full 179-classifier historical rerun is claimed.

**Confidence.** High in the error and moderately high in rejection severity. The original protocol and explicit overlapping historical partitions directly establish test-label reuse; the exact calculation proves that the claimed protection from bias is false. Corrected historical rankings and the actual bias magnitude remain unknown, and independent external-test cases are expressly outside the demonstrated reuse. The central cross-data-set comparison nevertheless lacks the claimed validation.

**Artifacts and limits.** The mirror archive has SHA256 `646ef23935d40252a250cfa9b9ff80d3322002972643a8f0eefccfd9812dbb7e`; `institutional-crosschecks.json` records the eight independently matched historical files. `delgado-partition-check.py`, `partition-overlap-results.json`, `delgado-exact-n12.py` and `exact-selection-bias-n12-results.json` reproduce the overlap and exact calculation. Original classifier drivers, selected-parameter logs, fold predictions and the full accuracy matrix were not recovered from the dead author URLs. The recovered mirror and institutional files are not presented as a complete historical experiment reproduction.

findings.title: GLM stopping and coefficient freezing do not preserve the claimed optimality
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2014__accepted__v15-dhurandhar14a-01 — GLM stopping and coefficient freezing do not preserve the claimed optimality
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF8 (printed2614), Algorithm2's first two conditional branches; PDF9–10 (2615–2616), Sections3.2.2–3.2.3 explaining them. The affected claim is advertised in the abstractPDF1, Table2PDF6 and the GLM extension in Section3.2. PDF20 attributes the finance speedup specifically to the second shortcut.

**Claim.** After using Algorithm1 to extend the previous model's final IRLS weighted-least-squares problem, Algorithm2 either accepts that solution when the upper-tail probability of its saturated deviance is at most epsilon_D, or fixes all old coefficients when their one-step change is at most epsilon_beta and optimizes only new coefficients. The paper labels the resulting GLM update optimal and interprets the first test as reaching a satisfactory near-optimal solution. Logistic regression is explicitly included, with epsilon_D=epsilon_beta=.1 in experiments. There is no assumption excluding the following finite, full-rank Bernoulli designs.

**Error and evidence.** The two shortcut tests are not optimization certificates. Here are two exact count-specified data sets; within each group, observations have the stated binary feature and the stated number of actual0/1responses. No stochastic generation, missing artifact or historical-rerun assumption is required. To isolate the error, grant Algorithm1 a correct exact WLS/Schur implementation, even correcting its separately missing weight factor.

### First branch accepts a fit far worse than the previous model

Start with an intercept-only logistic model, and then add a binary feature x:

| x | Observations | Responses equal1 | Responses equal0 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
|0|990000|1|989999|
|1|10000|2500|7500|

N=1000000. All four cells are positive, so the old and new logistic MLEs are finite and unique; the new two-column design has full rank. The exact old fitted probability is p=2501/1000000 and intercept a=logit(p)=−5.98856049436…. Write V=p(1−p)=2494744999/10^12. The old working response is z=a+(y−p)/V. Its WLS weight is a positive scalar constant across observations; either the paper's reciprocal-variance notation or the usual logistic variance-weight convention gives the same WLS fit in this example.

The extended WLS model has one free logit for each of the two groups. Its exact logits therefore equal the two group means of z:

    eta0 = a + (1/990000 − p)/V = −6.99066287356…
    eta1 = a + (1/4 − p)/V      = 93.21957504623… .

For logit eta with s successes among n ungrouped Bernoulli observations, negative log-likelihood is n*log(1+exp(eta))−s*eta. Evaluating this expression gives:

| Model | Negative log-likelihood |
|---|---:|
|Previous intercept-only MLE|17481.5225213|
|Algorithm2's extended WLS candidate|700064.616236|
|True full logistic MLE|5638.15690591|

The full MLE simply uses logits logit(1/990000) and logit(1/4). The candidate is consequently neither optimal nor a small approximation error: its loss is about40times the previous model's loss.

For these actual binary observations, saturated log-likelihood is0, so Algorithm2's tested deviance is D=1400129.232472…. Its specified reference law has nu=N−2=999998degrees of freedom. The chi-square upper-tail Chernoff bound gives

    Pr[chi_square(nu) >= D]
      <= exp(−(D−nu−nu*log(D/nu))/2)
      < exp(−31782.68) < .1 .

Thus the printed FIRST branch definitely accepts and returns the poor candidate, using exactly the paper's epsilon_D=.1. This calculation grants the paper's reference chi-square law for its algorithmic test; it does not require claiming that this law accurately describes binary-data deviance. Small upper-tail probability here signals large deviance, not closeness to the MLE.

### Second branch remains wrong even at zero coefficient-change tolerance

Reversing the first inequality alone does not repair optimality. Consider these30actual Bernoulli observations, with the old model again intercept-only:

| Newly added x | Observations | Responses equal1 |
|---|---:|---:|
|−2|10|1|
|−1|10|4|
|3|10|10|

The old intercept is0, and the new feature has mean0. The extended exact WLS/Newton step leaves the old intercept EXACTLY0 and gives new slope24/35. Its deviance is23.3159452…, with Pr[chi_square(28)>D]=.717070858…>.1, so the first branch is not taken. The SECOND branch then fixes intercept0 even if epsilon_beta is set to0.

Optimizing only the slope with this frozen intercept gives b=1.05074087512…. At that point the intercept likelihood score is

    sum_groups [successes − 10*sigmoid(x*b)] = 1.72968045689… != 0.

It is not a joint MLE. This is also an analytic sign argument: the constrained slope optimum is positive, and for every b>0,

    tanh(3*b/2) < tanh(b) + tanh(b/2),

so sigmoid(−2b)+sigmoid(−b)+sigmoid(3b)<1.5 and the intercept score is positive. The genuine full MLE is approximately(intercept1.46403463,slope1.85086658). Mixed responses in both negative-xgroups prevent separation and ensure a finite unique optimum. A zero first update of an old coefficient does not imply that it can be fixed throughout later nonlinear optimization.

Both examples concern the same underlying error: treating heuristic acceptance/freezing conditions as guarantees of an optimal GLM update. They count as ONE issue.

**Reason for rejection.** Extending efficient exact linear updates to accurate/optimal nonlinear GLM updates is the paper's central advertised contribution, rather than a peripheral utility. Algorithm2 can discard a much better previous model and terminate at a fit far from the available finite MLE; its other accelerated branch can fail even with zero coefficient-change tolerance. This invalidates the claimed accuracy-preserving shortcut on the paper's own model class. The correct OLS/Schur identity does not establish this extension. Restoring a safe optimizer requires replacing the deviance acceptance and allowing old coefficients to be reoptimized under a valid joint stopping test, changing both advertised shortcut regimes and requiring a new assessment of their speed/accuracy tradeoff. Merely tightening tolerances or reversing one inequality does not restore the stated result. The finding does not assert that efficient correct GLM updating is impossible, or that the original plotted numerical results have been falsified.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Section3.2, noticed that a goodness-of-fit tail probability was being used as an optimization certificate and that a zero one-step coefficient change was treated as persistent orthogonality. Constructed two-group and centered three-group logistic examples to test those implications.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the exact branching, deviance definition, tolerances, output and optimality claims against the original renderedPDF6/8/9/11/15 and full-paper context. Derived the first WLS step and full MLEs analytically; checked high-precision likelihoods and the rigorous chi-square tail bound; independently solved the second constrained score equation and evaluated its missing intercept score. A second reviewer read originalPDF8–11 and independently recomputed both examples at75digit precision, agreeing with the results and the centrality assessment. No original-code execution is claimed.

**Confidence.** **High.** Finite explicitly specified binary data satisfy rank/existence conditions; the first branch follows from an exact tail bound and the second fails at zero tolerance. Independent derivations agree. Confidence concerns the algorithm as written; unavailable historical code/data limit what can be said about actual implementation choices and figures.

 The initial correct WLS computation is explicitly granted; missing-weight/idempotence typos are not used to manufacture the counterexample.

Reason for rejection.

Extending efficient exact linear updates to accurate/optimal nonlinear GLM updates is the paper's central advertised contribution, rather than a peripheral utility. Algorithm2 can discard a much better previous model and terminate at a fit far from the available finite MLE; its other accelerated branch can fail even with zero coefficient-change tolerance. This invalidates the claimed accuracy-preserving shortcut on the paper's own model class. The correct OLS/Schur identity does not establish this extension. Restoring a safe optimizer requires replacing the deviance acceptance and allowing old coefficients to be reoptimized under a valid joint stopping test, changing both advertised shortcut regimes and requiring a new assessment of their speed/accuracy tradeoff. Merely tightening tolerances or reversing one inequality does not restore the stated result. The finding does not assert that efficient correct GLM updating is impossible, or that the original plotted numerical results have been falsified.

Discovery method.

While tracing Section3.2, noticed that a goodness-of-fit tail probability was being used as an optimization certificate and that a zero one-step coefficient change was treated as persistent orthogonality. Constructed two-group and centered three-group logistic examples to test those implications.

Verification method.

Rechecked the exact branching, deviance definition, tolerances, output and optimality claims against the original renderedPDF6/8/9/11/15 and full-paper context. Derived the first WLS step and full MLEs analytically; checked high-precision likelihoods and the rigorous chi-square tail bound; independently solved the second constrained score equation and evaluated its missing intercept score. A second reviewer read originalPDF8–11 and independently recomputed both examples at75digit precision, agreeing with the results and the centrality assessment. No original-code execution is claimed.

Confidence.

High. Finite explicitly specified binary data satisfy rank/existence conditions; the first branch follows from an exact tail bound and the second fails at zero tolerance. Independent derivations agree. Confidence concerns the algorithm as written; unavailable historical code/data limit what can be said about actual implementation choices and figures.

The initial correct WLS computation is explicitly granted; missing-weight/idempotence typos are not used to manufacture the counterexample.

findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2014__accepted__v15-doliwa14a-01 — A finite maximum class has minimum teaching dimension4 and VC dimension3
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF20 (journal3126), Theorem26 and its immediately preceding proof; paragraph following Corollary28 asserting that Tail Matching gives an order-VC teaching plan for every maximum class. Definitions of teaching sets/plans and maximum classes are on PDF4–6/9–10. Theorem29 on PDF21 uses Theorem26 in its proof. AbstractPDF1, introductionPDF3–4 and conclusionPDF23 advertise the all-maximum teaching-dimension result.

**Claim.** For every finite maximum concept class C, Theorem26 asserts

    RTD(C) = TS_min(C) = VC_dimension(C).

A maximum class is one attaining the Sauer cardinality bound on its finite domain. The teaching sets are ordinary correctly labelled examples distinguishing one concept from every other concept still present. The order of a teaching plan bounds all its teaching-set sizes; the first concept must be taught relative to the entire original class. No corner-peelability assumption restricts the theorem's domain. Its proof invokes a universal VC-size corner-peeling result; the paragraph after Corollary28 further asserts a universal acyclic Tail Matching representation that would induce the same size teaching plan.

**Error and evidence.** Let X={0,...,11} and let each integer below encode a concept by its12binary bits, with bit i the label at coordinate i. These299concepts constitute Hall's class from the primary ancillary [CH.txt](https://arxiv.org/src/1812.02099/anc/CH.txt), SHA256 `0367726b9934753a89711b42750d59f8a327860263383740ab85e6b6b27cc682`:
