findings.title: The sampled static MDP distribution is not the claimed exact Bayesian posterior
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2014__accepted__v15-tziortziotis14a-I01 — The sampled static MDP distribution is not the claimed exact Bayesian posterior
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pages 4–6 (journal2316–2318), §1.3/§2 and Algorithm1, especially the Bayesian update on line12; PDF pages8–10 (2320–2322), §2.2/§2.3, Eq2 and the update of every path model; PDF page11 (2323), §2.4.1 and Eq7, which independently sample the partition and local parameter pairs to form a fixed MDP; PDF page18 (2330), central exact-inference conclusion.

**Claim.** The paper defines a prior over stationary piecewise-linear Gaussian environments, updates it exactly in closed form, and samples an MDP from the resulting posterior for Thompson sampling. Its representation updates the conjugate regression at every node on the observation's path and samples a partition from stopping indicators, followed by local coefficient/covariance pairs from their respective conjugate distributions.

**Error and evidence.** A node's correct regression posterior depends on which observations were generated by that node under the sampled partition. Updating every ancestor on every matching observation and then sampling its regression independently of the partition loses that dependence. The following small example computes both distributions.

First grant the routine geometric and notation corrections most favorable to the method. Use the nearest-node ancestry actually implemented in the author's cited CoverTree class, and replace the printed descendant recursion by the intended ancestor recursion. The literal ball-membership definition on PDF7 does not itself define a single path; the example does not rely on that separate defect. Also grant the conventional, proper normal–inverse-Wishart density and correct local Student predictive distribution rather than the printed local formula slips.

Let the continuous state space be R with one action. There are two tree nodes, centered at0 and3/4. With cover base2, the child can be introduced at level−1: its distance3/4 is strictly greater than1/2 and less than1, satisfying separation/covering; the reduced depths are0 and1. At state0 the nearest-node path contains only the root; at state3/4 it contains child then root. The child is selected with prior probability q=2^-1=1/2. If selected, its region uses its own local regression; otherwise the root regression generates both regions.

For each node independently, use the same proper prior
```text
v_i ~ InverseGamma(shape=3, scale=1)
beta_i | v_i ~ N(0, v_i I_2)
x(s) = (s,1)^T
next_state | s,i,beta_i,v_i ~ N(beta_i^T x(s), v_i).
```
This is a one-output member of the intended matrix-normal/inverse-Wishart family, with coefficient mean0, input precision I_2, inverse-Wishart scale2 and conventional degrees6.

Observe transitions (state0,next0), then (state3/4,next0), and later (state0,next0), in **three separate episodes with externally specified start states**. These resets do not depend on the unknown dynamics. The first observation creates the root and the second creates the child, as allowed by the algorithm. Equivalently the child's coin may be drawn before the first observation: at the first start state0 the root generates the observation under either coin outcome, so this does not retrospectively assign root data to a new context.

For n zero responses and a design matrix X whose rows are x(s)^T, the integrated likelihood is exactly
```text
m(X,0) = Gamma(3+n/2) /
         [Gamma(3) (2*pi)^(n/2) sqrt(det(I_n + X X^T))].
```
Conditional on v the responses have covariance v(I_n+XX^T); integrating v against the stated inverse-gamma prior proves the formula.

After two observations, the likelihood if the child is selected is the product of two independent one-observation likelihoods. If it is absent, both observations use the root:

| Quantity | Exact value |
|---|---:|
| Single root determinant | 2 |
| Single child determinant | 41/16 |
| Joint root determinant for both observations | 33/8 |
| L_active,2 | 0.19411791692844127 |
| L_inactive,2 | 0.23508743090294698 |
| q_2 = L_active,2/(L_active,2+L_inactive,2) | 0.45227282909974315 |

Even granting the corrected weight update, which obtains this q_2 at the child, the root's posterior is **conditional on the partition**. When the child is selected, the root was trained by only the first observation; when it is absent, the root generated both. Thus the exact root posterior is a mixture of two conjugate distributions. The paper instead always uses the latter conjugate distribution and samples it independently of the child indicator. For example, the exact posterior E[v_root] is
```text
q_2*(1/(3+1/2-1)) + (1-q_2)*(1/(3+1-1))
= 0.3634848552733162,
```
whereas the all-path conjugate posterior has E[v_root]=1/3.

The third observation makes the erroneous inference directly observable in both an event probability and a predictive density. The determinant for two repeated root observations is3, and the determinant for all three observations under the root is91/16. Therefore:

| Quantity after the third, root-only observation | Exact static-MDP Bayes | Paper's all-path representation, even with corrected local recursion |
|---|---:|---:|
| Child selection probability | 0.42438130354346293 | unchanged at0.45227282909974315 |
| Predictive density of the third zero response, before observing it | 0.6267346896823583 | 0.6586494595586663 |

The exact three-observation likelihoods are L_active,3=0.11415767116985248 and L_inactive,3=0.15484020931326134. The event probability is their normalized active likelihood. The exact predictive density is (L_active,3+L_inactive,3)/(L_active,2+L_inactive,2); the paper's root regression instead gives L_inactive,3/L_inactive,2. The third update visits only the root, so it cannot change the stored child probability, although exact Bayes does.

All densities are positive and analytic. Strict discrepancies therefore persist on an open neighborhood of these responses; the finding does not depend on treating an exactly zero continuous response as an event with positive point probability.

**Reason for rejection.** Exact, online Bayesian inference over nonparametric stationary dynamics is a stated central contribution, explicitly distinguished from the separately approximate policy-optimization stage. The example disproves that inference claim and the claim that §2.4.1 samples its Bayesian posterior. Correcting the descendant labels, local conjugate density or cover-tree ownership does not recover the missing partition-dependent coefficient distributions. Exact static inference must retain the dependence of assignments, shared-root parameters and partition probabilities; alternatively the method must be recast as an adaptive mixture of predictive experts or an approximate posterior. That changes the claimed probabilistic contribution rather than correcting a notation or implementation constant. Empirical usefulness of the resulting heuristic does not establish the advertised exact posterior, so the paper as written warrants rejection on this central claim.

This issue does **not** assert a reversal of Figure3 rankings, invalidate every adaptive-expert predictor, or assert a Bayes-regret theorem that the paper never claimed.

**Discovery method.** Tracing the global fixed-MDP sampling interpretation to the local regression updates exposed that an ancestor learns observations generated by a selected descendant. This suggested testing whether a later observation in the root-only region should update the child selection probability.

**Verification method.** Rechecked original PDF pages7–11 and18, including rendered equations, Algorithm1 and Eq7. Read the official cited BVMM2010 pages2–4 and inspected its original theorem: its local active-expert recursion and distribution construction do not establish the static joint-posterior factorization needed here. Derived the collapsed normal/inverse-gamma likelihood and enumerated both partition outcomes. Forty-eight independent one-dimensional precision-integral quadratures for random designs/responses agree with the collapsed formula to relative error below5.44e−13. Inspected the author's recovered pre-publication Beliefbox implementation, commit7f2ccf34c31dc6d050eb4adc2f629a75c4d59fbd (2014-03-17): it trains every path regression and independently samples local models. A second reviewer independently checked the original central claims and the collapsed calculations at high precision.

 Running the Python control requires NumPy and SciPy; no historical benchmark reproduction is claimed.

**Confidence.** **High.** The claim is explicit in the original PDF, the discrepancy follows from closed-form likelihoods under proper permitted priors, and independent quadrature and reviewer calculations agree. The finding grants the obvious local corrections and remains false. Confidence concerns the central inference failure, not unrecovered historical experimental results.

findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Section7.1, assumptionsA1–A6, PDF19 (printed165); Section7.2, Steps1–4, PDF20 (166); definitions of rho0,rho1,rho2,rhoT and Theorem9/Equation7, PDF21 (167); the reduced-sample/weak-edge interpretation, PDF22–23 (168–169); AppendixE's application of Theorem26 to Step2, PDF40 (186).

**Claim.** Under a faithful minimal Gaussian model, A3 requires every full-graph nonedge to have some separator of size at most eta. A6 requires a decomposition V1,T,V2 with T separating V1 from V2 and |T|<eta. Step2 runs PC with conditioning size at most eta inside each Vk unionT. Theorem9 asserts consistent full-graph recovery whenever

\[
 n=\Omega\!\left(\max\{\rho_0^{-2}|T|\log p,
 \rho_1^{-2}\eta\log p_1,\rho_2^{-2}\eta\log p_2,
 \rho_T^{-2}\eta\log p_T\}\right).
\]

Here rho0 is the smallest nonzero partial correlation using at most |T| conditioning variables anywhere; rho1/rho2 minimize true-edge partial correlations using at most eta variables **inside their respective marginal subproblems**; rhoT uses true edges inT and the stated boundary conditioning domain. AppendixE imports the full-graph consistency analysis for these local problems. The required separator-size premise need not hold after marginalization, and the displayed rho quantities can all miss a genuine arbitrarily weak edge.

**Error and evidence.** The following exact construction satisfies every stated assumption and defeats the proposed transfer.

1. **A global five-separator becomes a local six-separator.** Let vertices be i=0,j=1,c1,...,c4=2,...,5,T={6,7,8,9},w=10. Set V1={0,...,5}, V2={10}. Include these edges and no others:

   - i-c and j-c for all four c;
   - i-6,i-7,j-8,j-9;
   - w-t for all four t inT;
   - the fixed edge6-7, which makes rhoT nonempty.

   Denote this graph by E. Edge i-j is absent. Every nonedge other than i-j has an endpoint of degree at most4, so its neighborhood is a separator of size at most4. For i-j there are five internally vertex-disjoint paths: the four paths through individual c's and i-6-w-8-j. Removing {2,3,4,5,10} separates them. Thus A3 holds with eta=5. Also T separates V1 from V2 and |T|=4<5, as required by A6.

   Step1 cannot delete i-j using at most four conditioning variables. Step2 restricts conditioning to A=V1 unionT, excluding w. Marginalizing w creates a clique onT. There are now six internally vertex-disjoint i-j paths in the marginal fill graph: the four c paths, i-6-8-j, and i-7-9-j. Equivalently, in the original graph every conditioning set S contained in A\{i,j} of size at most5 leaves an i-j path. Four removals are needed to block the four c paths, and two further removals are needed to block the remaining routes through w without conditioning on w.

   Therefore Step2 cannot delete i-j even with perfect independence tests and exhaustive search over all allowed local conditioning sets. The false edge survives finalStep4. Exact enumeration checks all219 allowed local sets. An independent graph-oracle implementation gives Step1 H=E union{i-j}; both the printed neighborhood search and a more generous exhaustive SGS Step2 retain i-j. The failure is independent of the printed PC neighborhood-pruning defect.

2. **A faithful Gaussian family verifies the distributional assumptions.** Let A_E be the adjacency matrix of E and put

\[
 Q_\epsilon=I-A_E/20-\epsilon(e_i e_j^\top+e_j e_i^\top),
 \qquad P_\epsilon=N(0,Q_\epsilon^{-1}),\quad
 0\le\epsilon\le1/20.
\]

   Each Q_epsilon is strictly diagonally dominant with negative edge off-diagonals: its eigenvalues lie in[13/20,27/20]. Its minimal graph is E at epsilon0 and E union{i-j} at epsilon>0. Faithfulness is exact: after conditioning on S, the precision on unconditioned coordinates is the corresponding principal submatrix. Its inverse has a convergent Neumann series with nonnegative terms, and its uv entry is positive exactly when u,v remain connected. Thus conditional independence is equivalent to separation, proving A1/A2 rather than relying on generic faithfulness. The uniform spectral bounds also supply A4's bounded variances and a fixed correlation bound M<1.

3. **All four advertised signal parameters stay positive while a true edge disappears statistically.** Adding i-j changes no separation pattern for conditioning sets of size at most4. If an endpoint is conditioned on, the new edge disappears. Otherwise i,j are already connected after any such deletion by their five disjoint paths, so adding their edge cannot merge previously separate components. Exact enumeration verifies all14,080 pair/set patterns. The nonzero tests entering rho0 therefore have the same zero/nonzero pattern at epsilon0 and epsilon>0; their finite positive minimum remains bounded below for small epsilon.

   Every fixed true-edge test entering rho1,rho2,rhoT is also strictly positive at epsilon0. The new true edge i-j enters rho1 for epsilon>0, but all its allowed local conditioning sets have size at most5; none separates it at epsilon0 by the preceding six-path argument. Hence its partial correlations also have a positive limiting minimum. Finiteness and continuity prove common positive lower bounds for all four rho parameters. Numerical checks give limiting minima approximately rho0=6.3289e-6, rho1 including i-j=1.2642e-5, rho2=.0500633, rhoT=.05; these numerical values supplement the exact positivity argument.

   Pad with independent unit Gaussian coordinates to p_n=n and assign padding to V2. A1–A6 still hold, including A5's growing dimension; the independent coordinates add only zero cross-component tests and do not reduce positive rho minima. Eta=5 is an allowed upper bound under A3, which does not require it to be the smallest possible bound for each graph. All four signal parameters stay bounded away from zero, p1=10 and pT=7 remain fixed, and p2 grows at most linearly. Thus the displayed sufficient condition is satisfied along n tending to infinity: its right side is O(log n), both for P0 and P_{1/n}.

4. **The claimed sufficient bound cannot support consistent recovery on both admitted sequences.** This is stronger than an incorrect oracle search. Let Sigma0=Q0^-1 and H=Sigma0^(1/2)(Q_epsilon-Q0)Sigma0^(1/2). Gershgorin gives lambda_min(Q0)>=7/10, so rank(H)<=2 and ||H||<=10epsilon/7. The Gaussian divergence is

\[
 D_{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\epsilon)
 =\tfrac12\{\operatorname{tr}H-\log\det(I+H)\}.
\]

   For |x|<=h<1, x-log(1+x)<=x²/[2(1-h)]. Consequently D_KL<=2epsilon² for epsilon<=1/20. With epsilon_n=1/n, the n-observation divergence is at most2/n, so total variation tends to zero. A common data-based graph estimator cannot recover both E and E union{i-j} with probability tending to1: otherwise testing whether its output contains i-j would distinguish two distributions whose total variation tends to zero. Both sequences satisfy the theorem's displayed sufficient condition with fixed positive bounds. Its general sample-complexity guarantee is therefore false.

   The missing signal is explicit. For the global five-cut {2,3,4,5,10}, exact symbolic inversion gives rho_ij|S²=(38000/37611)epsilon². For the local six-cut {2,3,4,5,6,7}, it gives rho_ij|S²=(199/198)epsilon². The former is excluded from rho0 because |T|=4; the latter is excluded from rho1 because eta=5. Neither weak correlation is controlled by Equation7.

**Reason for rejection.** Section7 explicitly identifies Theorem9 as the main theoretical result and uses it to justify the advertised lower sample requirement and weak-edge advantage of junction-tree decomposition. AppendixE reuses a global separator premise on local marginal problems where it is false. The stated rate can omit an arbitrarily weak true edge altogether, so a larger numerical constant cannot correct it. Increasing local search size introduces precisely the tiny correlations missing from the theorem; the bound must then include a different signal parameter and an epsilon^-2 requirement. Adding local-separator assumptions narrows the admitted graph class, while conditioning globally withdraws the claimed local statistical advantage for the problematic edge. Those are substantive changes to the principal guarantee, sufficient to change accept to reject for the paper as written. The framework's structural decomposition, suitable-family implementations and empirical results may remain useful.

**Discovery method.** While tracing AppendixD/E, an exact graph oracle first exposed that the endpoint-neighborhood PC search need not find separators promised by globalA3. Assessing the apparent exhaustive-search repair led to checking whether A3 is inherited by marginal subproblems; the five-versus-six separator construction then exposed the central transfer failure.

**Verification method.** Read all45 original pages and appendices; rechecked rendered PDF18–21/40 against the exact definitions, algorithm and theorem. Exact graph separation enumerations verified A3, both oracle searches and all small-conditioning zero patterns. A diagonal-dominance/Neumann-series argument establishes faithful Gaussian assumptions and uniform bounds for all n. Symbolic precision inversion checks the omitted weak correlations and KL expansion. Independent bounded review re-read originalPDF19–23/40 and inspected rendered19/20/21/40, independently reconstructing the graph, correlations and divergence argument. Authentic author2016 software types1/2 also retain the false edge on an exact-population-covariance control, with no claim that this deterministic mechanism control reproduces historical experiments.

**Confidence.** High mathematical confidence; moderately high rejection confidence. The construction meets the original model and dimension assumptions and has exact graph/analytic/symbolic certificates plus independent bounded QA. The uniform-rate impossibility and ideal-oracle failure are distinct checks. The conclusion is confined to the published general sample guarantee; it does not claim that every junction-tree algorithm fails or that historical tables have been disproved.

**Reproduction artifacts.**  Run `local-separator-controls.py`, `local-kl-controls.py`, and the independent `genton-local-separator-qa.py`; their saved JSON/output files contain the graph, separators, rho checks, exact formulas and divergence controls. `local-native-controls.m` and its output document the bounded author-code mechanism control and compatibility limits.

sections.html: The junction-tree method consistently recovers the graph under the stated global separator and signal assumptions.

sections.title: What may be wrong
sections.html: A separator available in the full graph can disappear from a local marginal graph. The local algorithm may then retain a false edge even with perfect tests.

sections.title: Evidence in brief
sections.html:
The audit constructs an 11-node graph where the relevant full-graph separator has size 5 but the local problem requires 6 conditioning variables. All 219 permitted local tests fail to separate the pair.

Adding an arbitrarily weak edge leaves the four advertised signal parameters bounded away from zero. The theorem then predicts recovery for graph sequences whose data distributions become statistically indistinguishable.

findings.title: The bounded sparse AC models cannot approximate the bounded comparator
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2014__accepted__v15-wang14b__I01 — The bounded sparse AC models cannot approximate the bounded comparator
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem 5(ii), PDF p.11 (printed p.1685), especially case 1; strategy §3.1, PDF p.9; definitions/assumptions, PDF pp.5–7; Appendix C.2, PDF p.27 (printed p.1701), last paragraph. The same error affects the AC upper bound in Corollary 10(ii), PDF p.15, using the regression strategy on PDF p.14. Proposition 15(ii), PDF p.24, displays the restricted approximation distance that the proof fails to control.

**Claim.** Under bounded truth $\|f_0\|_\infty\le L$, dictionary atoms satisfying only $\|f_j\|_{L_2(P_X)}\le1$, and the stated AC noise assumptions, the proposed AC strategies satisfy, in case 1,

\[
 R(\widehat f;f_0;n)\le C_1\operatorname{REG}(m_*)+
 C_0\left\{d^2(f_0;F_q^L(t_n))+C_2\sigma^2\frac{\log(1+t_n)}n\right\}.
\]

The constants are independent of $n,M_n,t_n,q$ and $f_0$; $C_0=1$ for AC-C. In Step II every AC model is

\[
 F^L_{J,s}=\left\{\sum_{j\in J}\theta_j f_j:
 \|\theta\|_1\le s,\quad\left\|\sum_{j\in J}\theta_jf_j\right\|_\infty\le L\right\},
 \qquad |J|\le M_n\wedge n.
\]

Step III combines their fitted estimates and zero by Catoni or ARM mixing. Theorem 13 supplies sparse $L_2$ approximations with an $\ell_1$ bound, but does not preserve this additional uniform bound.

**Error and evidence: exact family under every stated assumption.** For each even $n$, set $M=M_n=n+1$, $a=1/2$, $B=M^2$ and $\delta=M^{-4}$. On the finite input space $\{0,1,\ldots,M\}$, let

\[
 P_X(0)=1-\delta,\qquad P_X(i)=\delta/M\quad(1\le i\le M),
\]

and define

\[
 f_j(0)=a,\qquad
 f_j(i)=a+B\bigl(\mathbf1\{i=j\}-1/M\bigr),\quad 1\le j,i\le M.
\]

All atoms are finite measurable functions, and all input points have positive probability. Direct summation gives

\[
 \|f_j\|_2^2=\frac14+\delta B^2\frac{M-1}{M^2}
 =\frac14+\frac{M-1}{M^2}\le\frac12<1.
\]

Take $f_0\equiv1/2$, the known bound $L=1$, $q=1$, $t_n=1$, and independent $N(0,1)$ errors. These satisfy BD, the random-design model and the AC-C exponential-moment assumptions with constants fixed across the family. They also satisfy the Gaussian special case of AC-Y. Moreover,

\[
 f_0=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M f_j,\qquad
 \left\|(1/M,\ldots,1/M)\right\|_1=1,
\]

so $f_0\in F_1^L(1)$ and the asserted approximation error is exactly zero.

Now take **any** function in **any** Step II model. Its support $J$ has size at most $n<M$, so some $i\notin J$. Write $S=\sum_{j\in J}\theta_j$. At this omitted input point,

\[
 f_\theta(i)=(a-B/M)S=(1/2-M)S.
\]

The model's uniform bound $\|f_\theta\|_\infty\le1$ therefore forces

\[
 |S|\le\frac1{M-1/2},\qquad
 |f_\theta(0)|=|aS|\le\frac1{2M-1}.
\]

This restriction holds for every radius $s$, every training sample and every selected coefficient vector. It applies to the actual cited AC estimator: Audibert–Catoni's invoked Theorem 4.1, PDF pp.25–27 of [the 2010 preprint](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0902.1733v2), draws the fitted function from its model $F$; its deterministic posterior average also lies in the convex model. The related preprint at the arXiv identifier printed in the journal reference has the same support property. Catoni's final aggregation, Theorem 3.6.1 in the [author's lecture-note draft](https://ocatoni.perso.math.cnrs.fr/saintFlourDraft.ps), returns an average $E_\rho f$ with $\rho$ a probability. ARM likewise uses normalized nonnegative weights. Thus zero and every candidate obey the displayed cap at 0, and every possible final mixture does too. Subsequent clipping cannot remove the cap.

Consequently, even before taking expectation over training data or estimator randomization,

\[
 R(\widehat f;f_0;n)\ge
 (1-M^{-4})\left(\frac12-\frac1{2M-1}\right)^2
 \longrightarrow\frac14.
\]

In contrast, for $q=t_n=\sigma=1$ and $M=n+1$, the paper's effective model size is of order $\sqrt{n/\log n}$, so $\operatorname{REG}(m_*)=O(\sqrt{\log n/n})\to0$. Theorem 5(ii)'s right-hand side is therefore

\[
 C_1 O(\sqrt{\log n/n})+C_0C_2\log2/n\longrightarrow0
\]

for every fixed choice of its permitted constants. This contradicts the positive lower bound for the proposed estimator. There is no failed rerun or missing artifact in this argument.

**The literal bounded-design version fails too.** A second family satisfies the extra assumption $\sup_j\|X_j\|_\infty\le1$ in Corollary 10. Set $M=2n$. Give probability $1/2$ to a common input 0 and distribute the remaining $1/2$ uniformly over all $n$-element subsets $V\subset\{1,\ldots,M\}$. Define

\[
 f_j(0)=1/2,\qquad f_j(V)=\mathbf1\{j\in V\}.
\]

Each atom has sup-norm 1 and squared $L_2$ norm $3/8$. Their full uniform average is $f_0\equiv1/2$, with coefficient $\ell_1$ norm 1. Choose the legitimate known truth bound $L=1/2$. For any support $J$ of size at most $n$, some $V$ contains $J$, giving $f_\theta(V)=S$. The imposed cap implies $|S|\le1/2$ and hence $|f_\theta(0)|\le1/4$. All final mixtures have risk at least $\frac12(1/2-1/4)^2=1/32$, while the asserted rate again vanishes. To express this directly as regression, take the vector of these atom values as the covariates and use the coordinate predictors. No SRC assumption is needed for the corollary's upper bound. Choosing a larger configured bound can fix this second particular example; it does not validate the original assertion for the stated legitimate $L$.

**Why the proof fails.** Proposition 15(ii) correctly retains $d^2(f_0;F^L_{J,s})$. Appendix C.2 observes $\|\theta\|_1\le\|\theta\|_q$ and then imports the T-strategy approximation argument. That observation deals with the coefficient radius only. It does not establish that a sparse approximant lies in the bounded model. In the first family, every such bounded sparse approximant has a positive error, so the missing implication is false, not merely unproved.

**Reason for rejection.** Adaptive optimal aggregation over arbitrary dictionaries is a central contribution stated in the abstract, and Theorem 5 is its main upper-bound result. The AC branch is specifically claimed to retain the optimal rates while giving a sharp approximation constant and relaxing Gaussian known-variance restrictions. Here that actual strategy is inconsistent on an admitted bounded truth, even under benign Gaussian noise, rather than merely missing its optimal rate. Its general sharp aggregation guarantee and the literal AC regression upper bound cannot be accepted as written.

The T strategies, metric-entropy/sparse-approximation theorem and matching lower-bound constructions are not refuted. Nevertheless, preserving those results does not establish the advertised AC extension. Enlarging every candidate cap by a fixed factor does not resolve the general issue: in the first family a fixed cap $K$ gives $|\widehat f(0)|\le K/(2M-1)$, still tending to zero. Allowing the cap to grow with the spikes loses the uniform constants used by the AC oracle. Fitting clipped sparse linear functions changes the proposed convex linear class into a nonlinear class, to which the invoked AC $m/n$ theorem cannot simply be applied. Such a replacement needs a new estimator/analysis; it is not a local correction preserving the demonstrated theorem. This report makes no impossibility claim about other aggregation procedures.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the transfer from sparse approximation to the AC oracle, noticed that Theorem 13 preserves an $\ell_1$ bound but not the Step II sup-norm constraint. Built atoms whose large off-support values cancel only in the full average, then checked the actual estimator output class. The bounded-design construction was a subsequent strengthening.

Exact location.

Theorem 5(ii), PDF p.11 (printed p.1685), especially case 1; strategy §3.1, PDF p.9; definitions/assumptions, PDF pp.5–7; Appendix C.2, PDF p.27 (printed p.1701), last paragraph. The same error affects the AC upper bound in Corollary 10(ii), PDF p.15, using the regression strategy on PDF p.14. Proposition 15(ii), PDF p.24, displays the restricted approximation distance that the proof fails to control.

Claim.

Under bounded truth \(\|f_0\|_\infty\le L\), dictionary atoms satisfying only \(\|f_j\|_{L_2(P_X)}\le1\), and the stated AC noise assumptions, the proposed AC strategies satisfy, in case 1,

\[ R(\widehat f;f_0;n)\le C_1\operatorname{REG}(m_*)+ C_0\left\{d^2(f_0;F_q^L(t_n))+C_2\sigma^2\frac{\log(1+t_n)}n\right\}. \]

The constants are independent of \(n,M_n,t_n,q\) and \(f_0\); \(C_0=1\) for AC-C. In Step II every AC model is

\[ F^L_{J,s}=\left\{\sum_{j\in J}\theta_j f_j: \|\theta\|_1\le s,\quad\left\|\sum_{j\in J}\theta_jf_j\right\|_\infty\le L\right\}, \qquad |J|\le M_n\wedge n. \]

Step III combines their fitted estimates and zero by Catoni or ARM mixing. Theorem 13 supplies sparse \(L_2\) approximations with an \(\ell_1\) bound, but does not preserve this additional uniform bound.

Error and evidence: exact family under every stated assumption.

For each even \(n\), set \(M=M_n=n+1\), \(a=1/2\), \(B=M^2\) and \(\delta=M^{-4}\). On the finite input space \(\{0,1,\ldots,M\}\), let

\[ P_X(0)=1-\delta,\qquad P_X(i)=\delta/M\quad(1\le i\le M), \]

and define

\[ f_j(0)=a,\qquad f_j(i)=a+B\bigl(\mathbf1\{i=j\}-1/M\bigr),\quad 1\le j,i\le M. \]

All atoms are finite measurable functions, and all input points have positive probability. Direct summation gives

\[ \|f_j\|_2^2=\frac14+\delta B^2\frac{M-1}{M^2} =\frac14+\frac{M-1}{M^2}\le\frac12<1. \]

Take \(f_0\equiv1/2\), the known bound \(L=1\), \(q=1\), \(t_n=1\), and independent \(N(0,1)\) errors. These satisfy BD, the random-design model and the AC-C exponential-moment assumptions with constants fixed across the family. They also satisfy the Gaussian special case of AC-Y. Moreover,

\[ f_0=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M f_j,\qquad \left\|(1/M,\ldots,1/M)\right\|_1=1, \]

so \(f_0\in F_1^L(1)\) and the asserted approximation error is exactly zero.

Now take any function in any Step II model. Its support \(J\) has size at most \(n<M\), so some \(i\notin J\). Write \(S=\sum_{j\in J}\theta_j\). At this omitted input point,

\[ f_\theta(i)=(a-B/M)S=(1/2-M)S. \]

The model's uniform bound \(\|f_\theta\|_\infty\le1\) therefore forces

\[ |S|\le\frac1{M-1/2},\qquad |f_\theta(0)|=|aS|\le\frac1{2M-1}. \]

This restriction holds for every radius \(s\), every training sample and every selected coefficient vector. It applies to the actual cited AC estimator: Audibert–Catoni's invoked Theorem 4.1, PDF pp.25–27 of the 2010 preprint, draws the fitted function from its model \(F\); its deterministic posterior average also lies in the convex model. The related preprint at the arXiv identifier printed in the journal reference has the same support property. Catoni's final aggregation, Theorem 3.6.1 in the author's lecture-note draft, returns an average \(E_\rho f\) with \(\rho\) a probability. ARM likewise uses normalized nonnegative weights. Thus zero and every candidate obey the displayed cap at 0, and every possible final mixture does too. Subsequent clipping cannot remove the cap.

Consequently, even before taking expectation over training data or estimator randomization,

\[ R(\widehat f;f_0;n)\ge (1-M^{-4})\left(\frac12-\frac1{2M-1}\right)^2 \longrightarrow\frac14. \]

In contrast, for \(q=t_n=\sigma=1\) and \(M=n+1\), the paper's effective model size is of order \(\sqrt{n/\log n}\), so \(\operatorname{REG}(m_*)=O(\sqrt{\log n/n})\to0\). Theorem 5(ii)'s right-hand side is therefore

\[ C_1 O(\sqrt{\log n/n})+C_0C_2\log2/n\longrightarrow0 \]

for every fixed choice of its permitted constants. This contradicts the positive lower bound for the proposed estimator. There is no failed rerun or missing artifact in this argument.

The literal bounded-design version fails too. A second family satisfies the extra assumption \(\sup_j\|X_j\|_\infty\le1\) in Corollary 10. Set \(M=2n\). Give probability \(1/2\) to a common input 0 and distribute the remaining \(1/2\) uniformly over all \(n\)-element subsets \(V\subset\{1,\ldots,M\}\). Define

\[ f_j(0)=1/2,\qquad f_j(V)=\mathbf1\{j\in V\}. \]

Each atom has sup-norm 1 and squared \(L_2\) norm \(3/8\). Their full uniform average is \(f_0\equiv1/2\), with coefficient \(\ell_1\) norm 1. Choose the legitimate known truth bound \(L=1/2\). For any support \(J\) of size at most \(n\), some \(V\) contains \(J\), giving \(f_\theta(V)=S\). The imposed cap implies \(|S|\le1/2\) and hence \(|f_\theta(0)|\le1/4\). All final mixtures have risk at least \(\frac12(1/2-1/4)^2=1/32\), while the asserted rate again vanishes. To express this directly as regression, take the vector of these atom values as the covariates and use the coordinate predictors. No SRC assumption is needed for the corollary's upper bound. Choosing a larger configured bound can fix this second particular example; it does not validate the original assertion for the stated legitimate \(L\).

Why the proof fails. Proposition 15(ii) correctly retains \(d^2(f_0;F^L_{J,s})\). Appendix C.2 observes \(\|\theta\|_1\le\|\theta\|_q\) and then imports the T-strategy approximation argument. That observation deals with the coefficient radius only. It does not establish that a sparse approximant lies in the bounded model. In the first family, every such bounded sparse approximant has a positive error, so the missing implication is false, not merely unproved.

Reason for rejection.

Adaptive optimal aggregation over arbitrary dictionaries is a central contribution stated in the abstract, and Theorem 5 is its main upper-bound result. The AC branch is specifically claimed to retain the optimal rates while giving a sharp approximation constant and relaxing Gaussian known-variance restrictions. Here that actual strategy is inconsistent on an admitted bounded truth, even under benign Gaussian noise, rather than merely missing its optimal rate. Its general sharp aggregation guarantee and the literal AC regression upper bound cannot be accepted as written.

The T strategies, metric-entropy/sparse-approximation theorem and matching lower-bound constructions are not refuted. Nevertheless, preserving those results does not establish the advertised AC extension. Enlarging every candidate cap by a fixed factor does not resolve the general issue: in the first family a fixed cap \(K\) gives \(|\widehat f(0)|\le K/(2M-1)\), still tending to zero. Allowing the cap to grow with the spikes loses the uniform constants used by the AC oracle. Fitting clipped sparse linear functions changes the proposed convex linear class into a nonlinear class, to which the invoked AC \(m/n\) theorem cannot simply be applied. Such a replacement needs a new estimator/analysis; it is not a local correction preserving the demonstrated theorem. This report makes no impossibility claim about other aggregation procedures.

While tracing the transfer from sparse approximation to the AC oracle, noticed that Theorem 13 preserves an \(\ell_1\) bound but not the Step II sup-norm constraint. Built atoms whose large off-support values cancel only in the full average, then checked the actual estimator output class. The bounded-design construction was a subsequent strengthening.

Re-read all original definitions, the strategy, Theorem 5/Corollary 10 and Appendices A–C; inspected the rendered original pages containing the claims and proof. Recovered the primary AC and final-mixing definitions. Verified the norm/target/cap formulas exactly with rational arithmetic, checked 672 finite subset linear programs for the first family, and checked 2,681 support containments plus 12 representative bounded-design linear programs. Independently reviewed bounded mathematical QA agrees with the first counterexample and the additional bounded-design algebra. These finite controls corroborate the analytic all-\(n\) proof; they are not a substitute for it.

The full original PDF remains the authority for the audited claims.

Confidence.

High mathematical confidence; moderately high rejection confidence. The deterministic output barrier, exact comparator and vanishing claimed bound directly contradict the stated estimator guarantee. The rejection assessment is confined to the central AC universal aggregation contribution, with the substantial surviving T/approximation/lower-bound results explicitly preserved.

findings.title: The proposed behavior-based function is not a GP covariance kernel
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2014__accepted__v15-wilson14a-I01 — The proposed behavior-based function is not a GP covariance kernel
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 10 (printed page 262), §4.1, the unnumbered definitions of \(D(\theta_i,\theta_j)\) and \(K(\theta_i,\theta_j)\), and the preceding assertion that this constructs a valid kernel. The GP posterior covariance and expected-improvement procedure using it are in §3.1–3.3, PDF pages 5–7. PDF page 19 (printed page 271), §5.2, fixes \(\alpha=1\). The abstract on PDF page 1, introduction on page 2, and conclusion on page 27 identify this new GP kernel as the first of two main contributions.

**Claim.** For same-support stochastic policies, define their trajectory laws \(P_i=P(\xi\mid\theta_i)\) and

\[
D_{ij}=\sqrt{\operatorname{KL}(P_i\|P_j)}+
\sqrt{\operatorname{KL}(P_j\|P_i)},\qquad
K_{ij}=\exp(-\alpha D_{ij}).
\]

The paper asserts that the exponential produces a valid covariance kernel, allowing a GP over expected returns and Gaussian posterior uncertainty for selecting policies. This includes \(\alpha=1\), used in all its experiments.

**Error and evidence.** This function need not be positive semidefinite, even with exact trajectory probabilities. Consider an admissible one-step MDP with real-valued states: the initial state is uniform on \([0,1]\), either of two actions \(0,1\) is selected, the next state is independently uniform on \([0,1]\), and the episode terminates. The reward is the selected action, so all returns lie in \([0,1]\). Let the three policies choose action 1 with probabilities

\[
(p_1,p_2,p_3)=(10^{-3},10^{-6},10^{-12})
\]

independently of state. Every trajectory law has the same support and finite pairwise KL divergence. Common continuous state-density factors cancel, giving exactly

\[
\operatorname{KL}(P_i\|P_j)
=p_i\log(p_i/p_j)+(1-p_i)\log((1-p_i)/(1-p_j)).
\]

These policies also fit the experimental softmax form and parameter bounds in §5.1: use the constant feature \(f(s)=15\), parameter 1 for action 0, and parameter \(1+\log(p_i/(1-p_i))/15\) for action 1. The latter parameters are approximately \(0.5395496814,0.07896602947,-0.8420680744\), all in \([-1,1]\).

At \(\alpha=1\), the paper's exact function gives

\[
K\approx\begin{pmatrix}
1&0.897289167930372754&0.841918542679071013\\
0.897289167930372754&1&0.995430602781116310\\
0.841918542679071013&0.995430602781116310&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

For the integer vector \(c=(1,-4,3)^T\),

\[
c^TKc=-0.017136554115347396966112215784338\ldots<0.
\]

This is a direct covariance contradiction: the claimed prior variance of the linear combination \(\eta(\theta_1)-4\eta(\theta_2)+3\eta(\theta_3)\) is negative. A 70-digit interval calculation of the logarithms, square roots and exponentials encloses the quadratic form strictly between \(-0.017136554115348\) and \(-0.017136554115346\); the sign is not a floating-point eigensolver artifact. For an immediately algorithmic consequence, the first two policies' covariance block is positive definite, but the standard conditional variance for the third is

\[
1-K_{3,1:2}K_{1:2,1:2}^{-1}K_{1:2,3}
=-0.00437128689030605755\ldots.
\]

The GP Gaussian uncertainty and real-valued expected-improvement calculation therefore fail on these allowed policies. The determinant is \(-0.0008518420707113769\ldots\), providing another check.

This counterexample grants exact evaluation, so finite-trajectory error or importance-sampling variance cannot explain it. PDF page 11's displayed estimator omits the square roots and normalizations; even granting a consistent estimator of the intended page-10 function leaves the failure intact. Interpreting the estimator instead as normalized unrooted symmetric KL also does not resolve the problem: \(\exp[-\operatorname{KL}_{ij}-\operatorname{KL}_{ji}]\) has minimum eigenvalue approximately \(-0.00293158509\) on the same policies. The cited [Moreno, Ho and Vasconcelos paper](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2003/file/0abdc563a06105aee3c6136871c9f4d1-Paper.pdf), §3, merely applies exponentiation to an unrooted divergence and supplies no general positive-semidefiniteness theorem that resolves this example.

**Reason for rejection.** A new GP kernel relating policies by trajectory behavior is an expressly central contribution, not an auxiliary bound. The proposed function cannot be the covariance of the claimed GP, and the associated uncertainty-driven policy search can yield a negative predictive variance on fully admissible policies. Consequently that central probabilistic construction and its BBK/combined-method posterior interpretation are invalid as written. Repair requires replacing or materially redefining the covariance and providing a compatible evaluation rule for unexecuted policies, with justification and validation for the replacement. A positive-semidefinite projection of one observed matrix or an unspecified diagonal addition is not the stated all-policy covariance construction. Correcting the displayed Monte Carlo estimator also leaves the exact obstruction in place. The separate MBOA mean method with a valid RBF covariance may remain useful; it does not establish the failed first contribution. This loss of a named central construction warrants changing acceptance to rejection for the paper as written.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the first central contribution from the GP model to §4.1, the assertion that exponentiating this symmetric divergence yields a valid kernel prompted a finite-distribution Gram-matrix search.

**Verification method.** Rechecked original rendered PDF pages 9–11, 14, 19 and 27, including both square roots, the exponential, the same-support qualification and experimental \(\alpha\). Constructed the one-step MDP and explicit bounded-parameter softmax realization; recomputed KL, the integer-vector quadratic form, determinant and conditional variance at 100-digit precision, with an independent 70-digit interval calculation. A bounded independent reviewer also re-derived the quadratic form at 90 digits, certified it with 80-digit interval arithmetic, checked the Schur complement and inspected the original assumptions and centrality statements; the results agree. Checked the literal unrooted alternative and the cited original source for a possible resolution. Continued through every remaining method and experiment. The reproducible calculation and full-coverage notes are saved in unpublished audit files, `mathematical-results.json`, and `whole-paper-notes.md` beside the audit ledger.

**Confidence: High.** The strictly negative interval-certified quadratic form is an explicit violation of a necessary covariance condition. The MDP satisfies the paper's finite-horizon, same-support and bounded-return conditions, and even the stated experimental softmax parameter bounds. Original equations and centrality statements were inspected directly. This finding makes no claim about which estimator or numerical safeguards an unrecovered historical implementation used, or about a historical reward-ranking reversal.

findings.title: The optimized error bound does not bound the published final classifier
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2014__accepted__v15-wu14a-I01 — The optimized error bound does not bound the published final classifier
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pages 9–13 (printed 3021–3025), §3.1.2, definitions of the posterior classifier \(H_{t,c}\), Equations (5)–(15), Theorem 1 and Algorithm 3; PDF pages 13–14, §3.2, the different final voting classifier. Algorithm 1 on PDF page 6 computes weak-classifier voting weights at lines 8/11 before updating instance weights at line 13. The claimed theoretical guarantee is an explicit first contribution on PDF page 3, appears in the abstract on page 1, and is repeated in the conclusion on page 19.

**Claim.** The paper presents the Bayesian update as minimizing an upper bound on the proposed strong classifier's training error through boosting iterations. Its proved bound is

\[
B_{t,c}=\sum_{y_i=c}\frac{1-P_{t,c,i}}{P_{t,c,i}}
+\sum_{y_i\ne c}\frac{P_{t,c,i}}{1-P_{t,c,i}},
\]

for the posterior-threshold rule \(H_{t,c}(x_i)=\operatorname{sgn}(P_{t,c,i}>1/2)\). The deployed classifier instead votes using \(\log((1-\epsilon_{t,v})/\epsilon_{t,v})\), a global training-error weight for each weak classifier. The proof does not establish equality between those two decision rules. They can disagree enough that the optimized quantity is smaller than the final classifier's error.

**Error and evidence.** The following example uses the paper's Gaussian HMM weak learners, positive variances, positive counts in every prediction/label cell, positive voting coefficients, and a feasible normalized probability model.

There are two classes, denoted 0 and 1, and two scalar modalities. Every observation sequence has length 2 and repeats its modality's bit twice. Use one-state Gaussian HMMs, a uniform initial class prior, and uniform initial instance weights. The latter are consistent with normalized Equation (7) at prior odds 1. The training examples are specified exactly by these multiplicities:

| Modality bits \((u,v)\) | Class 1 count | Class 0 count |
|---|---:|---:|
| \((0,0)\) | 1 | 10,000 |
| \((0,1)\) | 1 | 10,000 |
| \((1,0)\) | 1 | 20,000 |
| \((1,1)\) | 10,000 | 1 |

Thus \(N=50{,}004\). The per-class sample restriction intended on PDF page 7 is granted. One-state Baum–Welch gives the exact Gaussian maximum-likelihood mean and variance, with transition probability 1 and positive transition counts. For class 1 the mean in either modality is \(10001/10003\), with variance \(20002/100060009\). For class 0 the respective means are \(20001/40001\) and \(10001/40001\), with variances \(400020000/1600080001\) and \(300030000/1600080001\). Evaluating these Gaussian likelihoods shows that each weak learner predicts class 1 at bit 1 and class 0 at bit 0. All variances are strictly positive; the saved high-precision log-likelihood checks have large margins.

The first weak learner makes 20,003 errors and the second 10,003. Both error rates are below \(1/2\). Their voting weights are approximately 0.40534845 and 1.38601941, so the final classifier follows the second weak learner on every example. It therefore makes **10,003 training errors**, with no voting tie. These coefficients are fixed before the posterior/instance-weight optimization in the first round. Taking \(T=1\) is permitted by Algorithm 1; the first-round prefix is also within the purported iterative guarantee.

Now consider these positive posterior odds for class 1, in the table's pattern order:

\[
R=\frac{P}{1-P}=(1/1000,\;1/10,\;1/10,\;10).
\]

They are feasible even if the missing probability constraints in the optimization are enforced. Set \(A=\sqrt{10}\), \(D=\sqrt{1/1000}\), and, for both modalities, define the probabilities in the notation of Equations (9), (11) and (15) by

\[
P_2=\frac{1-D}{A-D},\quad P_1=A P_2,\qquad
P_4=\frac{A-1}{A-D},\quad P_3=D P_4,
\]

with identical \(Q\). Every probability is strictly between 0 and 1, \(P_1+P_3=P_2+P_4=1\), and the per-view likelihood ratios are \(A\) for bit 1 and \(D\) for bit 0. With prior odds 1, the conditionally independent model gives exactly the stated four posterior odds: \(D^2=1/1000\), \(AD=1/10\), and \(A^2=10\).

Equation (6) at this feasible point equals

\[
\begin{aligned}
B_{1,1}
&=(1000+10)+(10+1000)+(10+2000)+(1000+10)\\
&=5040.
\end{aligned}
\]

Consequently, an exact global minimizer of the stated bound objective must have \(B_{1,1}\le5040\). This remains true for an optimization constrained to recoverable normalized probability ratios, because the displayed point is feasible. But the final vote has 10,003 errors. The optimized quantity therefore **cannot be an upper bound on the final classifier's training error**. The posterior classifier here implements AND and makes only 4 errors, so Theorem 1 remains correct for the classifier it actually defines. The failure is transferring its guarantee to the different published voting rule.

This is a certificate within the proposed optimization domain, not a claim that the displayed fitted conditional probabilities equal empirical confusion frequencies. If those probabilities are interpreted as a generative model, all eight label/pattern combinations have positive probability, so the sample is admissible. An additional saved control uses the empirical class prior and its normalized Equation (7) weights: the within-class Gaussian estimates stay unchanged, the second weak learner still gets the larger positive vote, and the same error/bound contradiction remains.

There is also a separate obstruction within the same claimed derivation. Algorithm 3 first minimizes over unconstrained positive ratios and then says the conditional probabilities can be recovered. With class-1 pattern counts \((27,9,9,3)\), class-0 counts \((9,3,3,1)\), and uniform initial prior, Equation (12) reduces to \(\sum b_{uv}(3/q_{uv}+q_{uv})\). All four optimal products are \(q_{uv}=\sqrt3\), attainable with all four ratios \(3^{1/4}\). Every factorization of this constant product matrix forces equal output ratios within each view. Normalization then forces each common ratio to equal 1, contradicting product \(\sqrt3\). Thus Algorithm 3's probability-recovery step can have no solution. Dropping that step and treating the ratios as positive potentials preserves some weight arithmetic, but it does not repair the final-vote counterexample above. Similarly, adding probability constraints does not repair that counterexample.

**Reason for rejection.** The theoretical training-error guarantee is explicitly a central contribution and is used to justify the proposed co-boosting training and fusion rule. It does not apply to the classifier the paper actually returns; the exact HMM example shows its alleged bound can be less than that classifier's error, even granting valid probabilities and ideal minimization. Restoring a guarantee requires a new proof for the actual vote, or changing inference to a posterior/potential-score classifier with class-specific log-ratio coefficients and an intercept. That changes predictions on this example and changes the classifier behind the empirical evaluation. A local normalization or probability-recovery correction cannot preserve both the published classifier and the claimed guarantee. This invalid central justification warrants rejection of the paper as written, while leaving weighted HMM estimation, feature selection and the historical empirical accuracies unrefuted.

**Discovery method.** Tracing the stated guarantee exposed two distinct classifiers: the posterior-threshold rule in the proof and the global-error-weighted vote in inference. Checking the claimed ratio-to-probability recovery then exposed missing normalization constraints.

**Verification method.** Read all 24 pages and Appendix A; rechecked the original rendered definitions, objective, update equations, voting rule and algorithm order. Constructed the exact count table, computed one-state Gaussian HMM maximum-likelihood parameters and likelihood signs, counted vote errors, recovered strictly normalized per-view probabilities, and evaluated Equation (6) using rational arithmetic. Checked a second initialization consistent with Equation (7). An independent reviewer separately re-derived the Gaussian likelihood comparisons, normalization contradiction, feasible posterior odds, 5,040 bound and 10,003 vote errors, and checked original pages. Reproduction files are an unpublished audit file, `mathematical-results.json`, and `genton-final-vote-qa.py`/`-results.json` beside the audit ledger. No historical gesture-data rerun is claimed.

**Confidence: High on the error; moderately high on rejection significance.** Rational counts and a strictly feasible probability construction establish a large bound violation for the actual voting rule, with independent high-precision HMM checks. The paper's first-contribution and conclusion statements make the guarantee central. The distinction between the valid posterior-classifier theorem, the invalid transfer to the final vote, and unavailable historical empirical verification is explicit.

sections.title: Claim in the paper
sections.html: The co-boosting updates minimize an upper bound on the training error of the returned classifier.
sections.markdown: The co-boosting updates minimize an upper bound on the training error of the returned classifier.

sections.title: What may be wrong
sections.html: The theorem bounds a posterior-threshold classifier, but the algorithm returns a different weighted vote. A small bound for the first classifier need not control errors of the second.
sections.markdown: The theorem bounds a posterior-threshold classifier, but the algorithm returns a different weighted vote. A small bound for the first classifier need not control errors of the second.

sections.title: Evidence in brief
sections.html:
The audit builds an exact Gaussian hidden-Markov-model example with 50,004 observations. A feasible normalized posterior model has the following bound, while the published voting rule makes more errors:

\[ \text{posterior error bound}=5{,}040<10{,}003=\text{voting errors}. \]

The posterior-threshold classifier itself makes only four errors. The discrepancy therefore comes from changing the prediction rule, and survives normalization repairs.

sections.html: The training-error guarantee needs a proof for the actual vote or a changed classifier and renewed experiments. The audit does not individually refute the feature-selection method or historical accuracy figures.
